faqs.question: Can I drive with P0107?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for short trips, but drive gently and get it checked soon. If the engine stalls, runs very rough, or loses power badly, stop driving.

faqs.question: Will P0107 cause bad gas mileage?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can. A wrong MAP signal can make the engine run too rich or too lean, which often hurts fuel economy.

faqs.question: Can a dirty air filter cause P0107?
faqs.answer: Not usually by itself. A dirty air filter may affect performance, but P0107 is more often caused by the sensor, wiring, or a vacuum hose problem.

faqs.question: Do I need a new MAP sensor for P0107?
faqs.answer: Not always. Many cases are caused by a loose connector, damaged wiring, or a hose problem, so testing is better than replacing parts first.

faqs.question: Will P0107 pass inspection?
faqs.answer: In many states, a check engine light means it will fail emissions inspection. The code should be repaired and cleared before testing.

title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Circuit High Input
answer: P0108 means the engine computer is seeing a MAP or barometric pressure signal that is higher than expected, which can throw off fuel and timing calculations. The most common fix is replacing a faulty MAP sensor, cleaning a bad connector, or repairing wiring, usually costing about $150 to $400 at an independent shop.
meaning: The MAP sensor tells the engine computer how much pressure is in the intake manifold so it can calculate engine load. On some vehicles, the barometric pressure reading is combined with this circuit, so a bad signal can affect how the computer measures air pressure outside the engine too. When the voltage stays too high, the computer thinks the engine is under a different load than it really is. That can cause rich running, rough idle, hard starting, or poor acceleration.
safety_note: The car may keep running, but the wrong pressure signal can cause poor fuel control, stalling, or flooding on some engines. Stop driving if the engine runs extremely rough, stalls repeatedly, or the check engine light starts flashing.

causes.name: Faulty MAP sensor
causes.detail: A bad sensor often causes a constant high reading, along with rough idle, hesitation, or a hard-start condition. If the code returns quickly after clearing it, the sensor is a top suspect.
causes.check: With a scan tool, compare MAP voltage or pressure to key-on engine-off barometric pressure; if it is way off or stuck high, the sensor is likely bad.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or poor connector at the MAP sensor
causes.detail: A rubbed-through wire, loose plug, corrosion, or 5-volt reference problem can push the signal voltage too high. Intermittent symptoms or the code changing when you wiggle the harness point to this.
causes.check: Inspect the connector for bent pins, oil, water, or corrosion, and gently wiggle the harness while watching live data for spikes.

causes.name: Vacuum hose or intake problem affecting MAP reading
causes.detail: If the sensor uses a vacuum hose or sits on a cracked intake, the reading can become inaccurate and trigger drivability problems. This is more likely if there is also a lean code, rough idle, or hissing noise.
causes.check: Look for cracked hoses, loose intake ducts, or obvious vacuum leaks around the intake manifold and sensor port.

causes.name: Engine control module issue or incorrect reference signal
causes.detail: This is less common, but a problem with the ECU, shared sensor reference, or internal circuit can keep the MAP input high even when the sensor is good. It becomes more likely only after the sensor, wiring, and vacuum checks pass.
causes.check: Verify proper 5-volt reference and ground at the sensor; if those are correct and the signal still reads wrong, the module or harness may need deeper testing.

diy.summary: A basic DIY check only needs a scan tool, flashlight, and inspection tools for the intake and connector. If the wiring, vacuum hoses, and sensor look good, diagnosis can get tricky and a shop may need to test the circuit with a meter and lab data.
steps: Read and clear the code, then see if it returns right away
Inspect the MAP sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Check the intake tubing and any vacuum hoses for cracks or leaks
Compare MAP live data with key-on engine-off barometric pressure
Verify the sensor has proper power and ground
Replace the MAP sensor if it reads implausibly high and wiring is good
Retest and confirm the code does not return

costs.note: parts about $40-$150, labor about $110-$200
varies by damaged wire count and access

costs.repair: Smoke test and repair vacuum leak
costs.note: diagnostic time plus hose or gasket repair

costs.repair: Diagnose and repair ECU or shared circuit fault
costs.note: testing time can add up before parts are replaced

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, engine layout, and labor rates in your area.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0108?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and get it checked soon. If the engine stalls, runs very rough, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving.

faqs.question: What causes a MAP sensor code to read high input?
faqs.answer: The most common causes are a bad MAP sensor, damaged wiring or connector, or a vacuum/intake problem affecting the signal. Less often, the engine computer or reference circuit is the issue.

faqs.question: Can I fix P0108 myself?
faqs.answer: You may be able to if the problem is a loose connector, cracked hose, or easy sensor replacement. If wiring testing or computer diagnosis is needed, a shop is usually the better choice.

faqs.question: Will P0108 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: In many states it can fail because the check engine light is on and the readiness monitors may not be set. Even if it passes tailpipe numbers, the stored code is often enough to fail inspection.

faqs.question: Do I need to replace the throttle body for P0108?
faqs.answer: Not usually. This code points to the MAP or barometric pressure circuit, so the sensor, wiring, vacuum leaks, or control circuit should be checked first.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
answer: P0110 means the engine computer sees a problem in the intake air temperature (IAT) sensor circuit, which tells it how warm the incoming air is. The most common fixes are repairing damaged wiring or replacing the IAT sensor, typically costing about $120 to $350 at an independent shop.
meaning: The intake air temperature sensor helps the engine computer adjust fuel delivery and ignition timing based on the temperature of the air entering the engine. If the signal is missing, shorted, or out of range, the computer cannot accurately calculate the air density. That can cause a hard start, rough idle, poor fuel economy, or an illuminated check engine light. On many vehicles the IAT sensor is built into the MAF sensor, while on others it is a separate sensor in the intake tract.
safety_note: Most cars can still be driven short term, but the engine may run too rich or too lean and fuel economy can suffer. Stop driving if the engine starts stalling, runs very rough, or shows other severe drivability problems.

causes.name: Bad IAT sensor
causes.detail: A failed sensor often causes a steady check engine light, poor fuel economy, or rough running with no obvious wiring damage. This is more likely if live data shows an impossible temperature reading like -40°F or extremely high heat.
causes.check: Read live scan data and compare the IAT reading to outdoor air temperature after the car sits overnight.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, a code that returns after hitting bumps, or a reading that changes when the harness is moved point to wiring trouble. Corrosion, broken wires, or loose terminals are common near the air intake and engine cover.
causes.check: Inspect the connector for bent pins, corrosion, loose fit, or rubbed-through wiring, then wiggle-test the harness while watching live data.

causes.name: Dirty or faulty MAF assembly with built-in IAT
causes.detail: If the IAT is part of the mass air flow sensor, a MAF problem can trigger this code along with airflow-related driveability complaints. This is more likely if the vehicle also has lean codes or airflow-related symptoms.
causes.check: Check whether the IAT is separate or built into the MAF, and inspect the MAF for contamination or prior improper cleaning.

causes.name: Blown sensor circuit fuse or power/ground issue
causes.detail: A missing reference voltage or ground can set P0110 and usually shows up as a dead or fixed temperature reading. This is more likely if multiple engine sensor codes appear at the same time.
causes.check: Verify the sensor has the correct reference voltage and ground with a multimeter or wiring diagram.

diy.summary: If the IAT is a separate sensor and the issue is an unplugged connector or damaged pigtail, this can be a doable home repair with basic hand tools, a scan tool, and possibly a multimeter. If the sensor is built into the MAF or the wiring is hard to access, a shop diagnosis is often faster and safer.
steps: Check the intake sensor location and whether it is separate or part of the MAF
Inspect the connector and wiring for damage, oil, dirt, or corrosion
Compare live IAT data to outside air temperature after the car sits
Clear the code and see whether it returns immediately
Replace the sensor or repair the connector if the reading is clearly wrong
Repair any damaged wiring and secure the harness away from heat and movement

costs.note: parts about $20-$90, labor about $60-$130
diagnosis plus pigtail/connector repair

costs.repair: Replace mass air flow sensor with built-in IAT
costs.note: parts about $150-$400, labor about $80-$150

costs.repair: Diagnose power, ground, or PCM circuit fault
costs.note: diagnostic time only; extra repairs may apply

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, engine layout, and local labor rates, and dealer pricing is often higher.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0110?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but the engine may run poorly and waste fuel. Get it checked soon, especially if the idle gets rough or the car starts stalling.

faqs.question: Will P0110 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it may disappear if the problem was temporary, but the code usually returns if the sensor or wiring is actually bad. Clearing it without fixing the cause does not solve the issue.

faqs.question: Is P0110 the same as a bad MAF sensor?
faqs.answer: Not always. On some cars the IAT sensor is built into the MAF sensor, but on others it is a separate part and the MAF may be fine.

faqs.question: Can a dirty air filter cause P0110?
faqs.answer: A dirty air filter usually does not directly set this code, but it can contribute to airflow issues on vehicles with the IAT built into the MAF housing. The sensor and wiring should still be checked first.

faqs.question: Will P0110 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: It can, because the check engine light is on and the engine may not be managing fuel correctly. Most states will fail a vehicle with an active emissions-related code.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance
answer: P0111 means the engine computer is seeing an intake air temperature sensor signal that does not make sense for the conditions. The most common fix is replacing the intake air temperature sensor or repairing its wiring, usually about $100 to $300 at an independent shop.
meaning: The intake air temperature (IAT) sensor tells the engine computer how warm the air entering the engine is. The computer uses that information to adjust fuel delivery and ignition timing so the engine runs smoothly and efficiently. When the signal is out of range or changes in a way that does not match the engine’s actual conditions, the computer sets P0111. This can happen from a bad sensor, wiring problem, connector issue, or sometimes an air intake problem that makes the reading inaccurate.
symptoms: Stale or overly rich running smell
safety_note: This code usually will not leave you stranded right away, but the engine may run too rich or too lean, which can hurt drivability and fuel economy. Stop driving if the engine runs very rough, stalls, or the check engine light starts flashing.

causes.name: Bad intake air temperature sensor
causes.detail: A sensor that reads too high, too low, or changes erratically is the most common reason for P0111. Rough idle, hesitation, and no other obvious intake problems often point here.
causes.check: Look at live data with a scan tool; if the IAT reading is far outside outside temperature or jumps around, the sensor may be bad.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or loose connector
causes.detail: Broken wires, corrosion, or a poor connector fit can make the signal unstable and trigger a range/performance code. Intermittent symptoms or a code that returns after bumps or rain often point to this.
causes.check: Inspect the harness and connector for corrosion, bent pins, broken insulation, or loose fit and gently wiggle the connector while watching live data.

causes.name: Dirty, restricted, or modified air intake path
causes.detail: If the sensor is mounted in a hot spot, blocked by debris, or affected by an aftermarket intake or missing ducting, the reading may not match actual air temperature. This is more likely when the problem started after air filter or intake work.
causes.check: Verify the air box, ducting, and filter are installed correctly and that the sensor is in the proper location.

causes.name: Faulty engine computer input circuit
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring test good but the scan data is still wrong, the PCM circuit itself may be failing. This is less common and usually comes after other causes are ruled out.
causes.check: Have a shop test the sensor circuit for proper voltage and resistance before suspecting the computer.

diy.summary: A careful owner can inspect the sensor and connector, clean the connection, and replace the IAT sensor if it is easy to access. You will need a basic scan tool, multimeter, and the correct replacement sensor if testing shows the sensor is faulty.
steps: Read the code and check live IAT temperature data
Compare the IAT reading to outside air temperature after the car sits overnight
Inspect the sensor, intake tube, and wiring connector for damage or looseness
Repair any damaged wiring or dirty terminals
Replace the IAT sensor if the reading is still out of range
Clear the code and road test the car
Recheck live data to confirm the reading is stable

costs.note: parts about $20-$80, labor about $80-$220
depends on harness damage and access

costs.repair: Air intake duct, air box, or connector repair
costs.note: parts and labor vary with intake design
diagnosis first; module replacement is rare

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle design, rust, and local labor rates, and diagnostics may be separate from repair.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0111?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for short trips, but drive gently and get it checked soon. If the engine starts running very rough, stalls, or loses power badly, stop driving and have it towed.

faqs.question: Will P0111 cause bad gas mileage?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can. When the engine computer gets a bad air temperature reading, it may add too much or too little fuel.

faqs.question: Can I fix P0111 myself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. If the problem is a loose connector, damaged wire, or an easy-to-reach sensor, a DIY repair is possible with basic tools and a scan tool.

faqs.question: Will P0111 fail emissions or inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, because the check engine light is on and the engine computer has a fault stored. Some states will also fail the car if readiness monitors are not set after repairs.

faqs.question: Is P0111 the same as a mass air flow sensor code?
faqs.answer: No. P0111 is for the intake air temperature sensor signal range or performance, although on some vehicles the IAT reading may be part of another sensor assembly.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low
answer: P0112 means the engine computer is seeing an intake air temperature sensor signal that is too low, which usually points to a sensor or wiring problem. The most common fix is replacing the intake air temperature sensor or repairing damaged wiring, typically $100 to $300 at an independent shop.
meaning: The intake air temperature (IAT) sensor tells the engine computer how warm the air entering the engine is. That information helps the computer adjust fuel delivery and ignition timing for better starting, drivability, and emissions. When the circuit reads too low, the computer thinks the incoming air is much hotter than it really is, or the signal is being pulled down by a wiring fault. This can happen from a failed sensor, corrosion in the connector, or damaged wiring near the air intake.
safety_note: The car will usually still run, but fuel economy and drivability can suffer, and the engine may run too rich or too lean depending on the failure. Stop driving if the engine starts stalling, runs very rough, or the check engine light begins flashing.

causes.name: Bad intake air temperature sensor
causes.detail: A failed sensor is the most common cause, especially if the code returns right after clearing and the engine may run poorly or get bad fuel economy.
causes.check: Inspect the sensor for damage and compare live scan-tool intake air temperature to ambient temperature after the car has sat overnight.

causes.name: Corroded or loose connector
causes.detail: If the light is intermittent or the problem changes when the harness is moved, a bad connector is likely.
causes.check: Unplug the sensor and look for bent pins, green corrosion, moisture, or a loose fit.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or short to ground
causes.detail: A rubbed-through wire can hold the signal low all the time, which often causes an immediate code and may affect other intake-related readings.
causes.check: Inspect the wiring from the sensor to the engine harness for cuts, melted spots, or chafing near the air box and intake tube.

causes.name: Problem in the air intake housing or sensor mounting
causes.detail: If the sensor is loose, installed wrong, or contaminated with oil or dirt, the reading can be inaccurate and set the code.
causes.check: Make sure the sensor is seated correctly and the intake tract is intact and not heavily contaminated.

diy.summary: On many cars this is a simple sensor and connector inspection with a basic socket or screwdriver, plus a scan tool if you have one. If wiring repair is needed, it is still possible for a careful DIYer, but you need to trace and test the circuit correctly.
steps: Read the code and freeze-frame data.
Look at live IAT temperature after the engine has cooled overnight; it should be close to outdoor temperature.
Inspect the sensor connector for corrosion, loose pins, or broken lock tabs.
Check the wiring for rubbing, cuts, or melted insulation.
Unplug and reseat the connector, then clear the code and retest.
Replace the IAT sensor if readings are wrong and the wiring looks good.
Repair damaged wiring if the code returns after sensor replacement.

costs.note: parts about $20-$80, labor about $80-$220
depends on corrosion or how much harness repair is needed

costs.repair: Air intake duct or housing repair
costs.note: if the sensor mount or intake tube is damaged
shop test time before repair

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, location, and how hard the sensor and wiring are to access.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0112?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and get it checked soon. If the engine starts running very rough, stalling, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving.

faqs.question: What does “circuit low” mean on an IAT sensor code?
faqs.answer: It means the computer is seeing a signal voltage that is lower than expected. That is often caused by a bad sensor, a shorted wire, or a poor connection.

faqs.question: Can a dirty air filter cause P0112?
faqs.answer: A dirty air filter usually does not cause this code by itself. The problem is more often the sensor, connector, or wiring near the intake.

faqs.question: Will P0112 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can. A stored check engine light and an active intake air temperature fault can cause an emissions test failure in many states.

faqs.question: Is P0112 expensive to fix?
faqs.answer: Usually it is one of the cheaper check-engine codes to fix. Many repairs fall in the $100 to $300 range unless wiring damage is extensive.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
answer: P0113 means the engine computer is seeing an intake air temperature (IAT) signal that is too high, which usually means the sensor circuit is open, unplugged, or the sensor has failed. The most common fix is repairing the connector or replacing the IAT sensor, typically about $75 to $250 at an independent shop.
meaning: The intake air temperature sensor tells the engine computer how hot the air entering the engine is. That information helps the computer adjust fuel mixture and timing, especially during cold starts and hot weather. When the circuit reads too high, the computer usually thinks the intake air is extremely cold or the signal is out of range because the circuit is open. This can happen from a bad sensor, damaged wiring, a loose connector, or a problem with the intake tube or air box area where the sensor sits.
symptoms: Possible slightly rich or lean running
safety_note: The car usually still runs, but fuel control may be off and cold starts or drivability can get worse. Stop driving if the engine runs very rough, stalls often, or the check engine light starts flashing.

causes.name: Unplugged or loose IAT sensor connector
causes.detail: A loose connector often causes an immediate P0113, especially if the light came on after air filter, intake, or engine work. The code may come and go if the connection is intermittent.
causes.check: Inspect the sensor plug for looseness, broken tabs, corrosion, or a connector not fully seated.

causes.name: Damaged IAT sensor wiring or open circuit
causes.detail: Broken, rubbed-through, or corroded wires can make the signal read too high all the time or only when the engine moves. This is more likely if the code returns after clearing or changes when you wiggle the harness.
causes.check: Look for damaged wiring near the air cleaner, intake tube, or harness routing and gently wiggle-test the harness with the engine off.

causes.name: Faulty intake air temperature sensor
causes.detail: A failed sensor can set P0113 even when the connector and wiring look normal. This is common if the engine otherwise runs normally but the code comes back right away.
causes.check: Compare live IAT data to outside air temperature after the car sits overnight; a bad sensor often shows an unrealistic reading.

causes.name: Problem in the intake duct or air box area
causes.detail: If the sensor is built into the air intake duct or MAF assembly, cracks, moisture intrusion, or a loose sensor mount can affect the signal. This fits cases where the code started after an intake repair or air filter service.
causes.check: Inspect the intake tube, air box, and sensor mounting for damage, missing seals, or signs of water intrusion.

diy.summary: You may be able to fix this with basic tools, a flashlight, and contact cleaner if the problem is a loose plug or obvious wiring issue. If the sensor is part of another assembly or the wiring needs testing with a meter, ask the shop to diagnose the IAT circuit and verify the signal and reference voltage.
steps: Turn the key off and locate the IAT sensor and connector
Inspect the plug for looseness, corrosion, bent pins, or broken locking tabs
Check the wiring near the air intake for cuts, rubbing, or oil damage
Clear the code and see if it returns after a short drive
If available, view live IAT temperature with a scan tool and compare it to ambient temperature
Replace the sensor if the reading stays unrealistic and wiring looks good
Recheck for stored codes after the repair

costs.note: parts usually $20-$80, labor $55-$170
depends on harness damage and labor time

costs.repair: Air intake duct or sensor housing repair
costs.note: parts and labor vary by vehicle design
often credited toward repair at some shops

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, engine layout, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0113?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and get it checked soon. If the engine stalls, runs very rough, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving.

faqs.question: What is the most common fix for P0113?
faqs.answer: The most common fix is repairing a loose or damaged IAT sensor connector or replacing the sensor itself. On many cars the part is inexpensive, but wiring damage can raise the cost.

faqs.question: Will P0113 hurt fuel economy?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can. When the engine computer gets a bad air temperature signal, it may add or subtract the wrong amount of fuel.

faqs.question: Can I clear P0113 without replacing parts?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, if the code was caused by a loose plug or temporary wiring issue. If it comes back, the underlying fault still needs to be repaired.

faqs.question: Will P0113 keep my car from passing inspection?
faqs.answer: In many states, yes, because the check engine light is on and the readiness monitors may not complete. The code should be fixed and cleared before inspection.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Circuit
answer: P0115 means the engine computer is seeing a problem in the engine coolant temperature sensor circuit, so it cannot trust the engine temperature reading. The most common fix is replacing a bad coolant temperature sensor or repairing damaged wiring, usually about $120 to $350 at an independent shop.
meaning: The engine coolant temperature sensor tells the computer how hot the engine is. The computer uses that signal to adjust fuel mixture, idle speed, cooling fan operation, and in some cars transmission behavior. If the circuit has an open, short, bad connector, or a failed sensor, the reading can be wrong or disappear completely. That can cause hard starting, poor fuel economy, rough running, or overheating if the fans are not controlled correctly.
symptoms: Cooling fan running too much or not enough
Temperature gauge reading wrong or erratic
safety_note: The car may still run, but the wrong temperature signal can cause poor fueling, rough running, or cooling fan problems. Stop driving if the engine starts overheating, the temperature warning light comes on, or the gauge rises toward hot.

causes.name: Bad engine coolant temperature sensor
causes.detail: A failed sensor often causes a check engine light, hard starting, rough idle, or a temperature reading that jumps around or stays very cold or very hot.
causes.check: Use a scan tool to compare coolant temperature on a cold engine to outside air temperature; if it reads far off, the sensor may be bad.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or loose connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, a code that returns after bumps, or a reading that drops out completely often point to wiring or connector problems.
causes.check: Inspect the harness and connector at the sensor for corrosion, broken wires, coolant intrusion, or a loose plug.

causes.name: Low coolant or trapped air in the cooling system
causes.detail: If the sensor is exposed because the coolant level is low or air is trapped around it, the reading can be unstable and the engine may run oddly or overheat.
causes.check: Check the coolant level only when the engine is cold and look for signs of leaks or recent coolant service without proper bleeding.

causes.name: Engine computer issue or wrong reference voltage
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring test good but the code stays present, the computer may not be reading the signal correctly.
causes.check: A technician can verify sensor voltage and resistance directly at the connector before condemning the PCM.

diy.summary: A handy owner can inspect the connector, check coolant level, and sometimes replace the sensor with basic tools. You need the correct sensor for the engine, fresh coolant if any is lost, and a scan tool helps confirm the fix.
steps: Let the engine cool completely.
Check the coolant level in the reservoir and radiator if equipped.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion.
Read live coolant temperature with a scan tool and compare it to a cold engine.
Replace the sensor if the reading is clearly wrong and the wiring looks good.
Top off coolant and bleed air from the system as required.
Clear the code and road test.
Recheck for leaks and confirm the temperature reading is normal.

costs.note: parts about $20-$80, labor about $100-$200

costs.repair: Repair coolant sensor wiring or connector
costs.note: depends on wire damage and connector condition
if low coolant or air in system is the issue

costs.repair: Thermostat replacement if related cooling fault is found
costs.note: often found during diagnosis, not the code itself

cost_note: Prices vary by engine layout, coolant type, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0115?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and watch the temperature gauge. If the engine overheats or the gauge stops making sense, stop driving.

faqs.question: Will P0115 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it may come and go if the problem is loose wiring or an intermittent connector, but the code usually returns until the fault is fixed.

faqs.question: Can a bad thermostat cause P0115?
faqs.answer: A bad thermostat can cause temperature problems, but it does not usually cause this code by itself. P0115 is mainly about the sensor circuit, so the sensor, wiring, and connector should be checked first.

faqs.question: Is the coolant temperature sensor hard to replace?
faqs.answer: On some cars it is simple, but on others it is buried under intake parts or near the thermostat housing. If coolant must be drained or air bled from the system, the job is easier with experience.

faqs.question: Will P0115 cause bad gas mileage?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can. If the computer thinks the engine is cold all the time, it may add extra fuel and lower fuel economy.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Circuit Range/Performance
answer: P0116 means the engine computer thinks the coolant temperature signal is outside the normal range or is changing in a way that does not match engine warm-up. The most common fix is replacing a faulty engine coolant temperature (ECT) sensor or repairing its wiring, usually about $150 to $350 at an independent shop.
meaning: The engine coolant temperature sensor tells the computer how hot the engine is. The computer uses that signal to control fuel mixture, idle speed, cooling fan operation, and when the engine is considered warm. If the signal is inaccurate, stuck, or slow to respond, the computer can set P0116. This code can be caused by a bad sensor, low coolant level, corrosion in the connector, damaged wiring, or a thermostat problem that keeps the engine from warming up normally. On many cars, a failing sensor will make the temperature reading jump around, read too cold, or take too long to reach normal temperature. The check engine light may come on even if the car still seems to run mostly okay.
symptoms: Temperature gauge reading low or erratic
safety_note: If the engine temperature signal is wrong, the computer may run the engine too rich or too lean, which can hurt fuel economy and cause rough running. Stop driving if the temperature gauge shows overheating, the coolant warning light comes on, or the engine starts losing power or misfiring.

causes.name: Faulty engine coolant temperature sensor
causes.detail: A bad sensor often causes a cold-running reading, a stuck reading, or a reading that does not match the actual engine temperature. This is more likely if the light came on after the engine temperature reading became erratic.
causes.check: Compare the live coolant temperature on a scan tool to a cold engine and again after warm-up.

causes.name: Low coolant level or air pocket
causes.detail: Low coolant can keep the sensor from sitting in flowing coolant, which makes the reading unstable or incorrect. This is common if the car also has poor heat from the cabin heater or a recent coolant leak.
causes.check: Check the coolant level only when the engine is cold and inspect for leaks.

causes.name: Corroded or damaged sensor wiring connector
causes.detail: Loose pins, broken wires, or coolant intrusion at the connector can create an intermittent or unrealistic signal. This is more likely if the problem comes and goes when hitting bumps or moving the harness.
causes.check: Inspect the connector for green corrosion, bent pins, oil or coolant contamination, and damaged wiring.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open or slow to warm up
causes.detail: If the engine takes too long to reach normal temperature, the computer may see a range or performance problem even though the sensor is working. This is more likely if the temperature gauge stays low and the heater blows cooler than normal on the highway.
causes.check: Watch how long it takes to reach normal operating temperature on a scan tool or dash gauge.

diy.summary: A DIY fix is possible if the issue is low coolant, a loose connector, or an easy-to-access ECT sensor. You will need basic hand tools, a scan tool if possible, and the correct sensor or thermostat for the vehicle.
steps: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
Inspect the ECT sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion.
Read live coolant temperature data with a scan tool if available.
Compare the reading to a cold engine and after warm-up.
Replace the ECT sensor if it reads incorrectly and the wiring is good.
Clear the code and retest after the repair.
If the engine runs too cool, test the thermostat.
Bleed air from the cooling system if coolant was low or opened during repair.

costs.note: parts and labor; sensor is usually inexpensive, labor varies by access
includes diagnosis and minor wiring repair

faqs.question: Can I keep driving with P0116?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time if the engine is not overheating and it still runs normally, but you should get it checked soon. Do not keep driving if the temperature gauge rises too high, the heater stops working, or the engine starts running badly.

faqs.question: Will P0116 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: In many states it can, because the check engine light is on and the monitor may not be ready. The exact rules depend on your state.

faqs.question: Is the coolant temperature sensor hard to replace?
faqs.answer: On some cars it is simple and on others it is buried under intake parts or near tight hoses. If access is poor or coolant has to be drained, a shop may be the better choice.

faqs.question: Can low coolant cause P0116?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low coolant or trapped air can make the sensor read wrong because it is not fully surrounded by coolant.

faqs.question: Should I replace the thermostat or sensor first?
faqs.answer: Usually the sensor and wiring are checked first, because they are the most common causes. If the live temperature data shows the engine never warms up normally, the thermostat becomes more likely.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Circuit Low
answer: P0117 means the engine computer is seeing an abnormally low signal from the engine coolant temperature sensor circuit, usually because the sensor, wiring, or connector is faulty. The most common fix is replacing the coolant temperature sensor or repairing the connector/wiring, typically costing about $120 to $350 at an independent shop.
meaning: The engine coolant temperature sensor tells the computer how hot the engine is so it can control fuel mixture, idle speed, fan operation, and emission systems. When the circuit reads too low, the computer may think the engine is colder than it really is. That can lead to rich fuel mixture, hard starting, poor fuel economy, and higher emissions. In some cases the problem is not the sensor itself, but a damaged wire, corroded connector, or low coolant affecting the sensor reading.
symptoms: Black exhaust smoke or fuel smell
Cooling fans running more than normal
safety_note: The car will usually still run, but the engine may run too rich and waste fuel or foul spark plugs. Stop driving if the engine starts overheating, runs very rough, or you lose cabin heat because the cooling system is low on coolant.

causes.name: Faulty engine coolant temperature sensor
causes.detail: A bad sensor commonly causes a false cold reading, which fits a check engine light, rich running, hard starting, or poor mileage. If the dash gauge and scan data disagree, the sensor is a strong suspect.
causes.check: Compare live coolant temperature on a scan tool with engine temperature after warm-up; a reading that stays very low or jumps around points to the sensor.

causes.name: Corroded or loose sensor connector
causes.detail: Intermittent rough idle, sudden fan operation, or a code that comes and goes often points to a bad connection at the sensor. Green corrosion, broken locks, or coolant in the plug are clues.
causes.check: Inspect the connector for corrosion, bent pins, loose fit, or coolant intrusion and wiggle-test the harness with the engine idling.

causes.name: Wiring short to ground or damaged harness
causes.detail: A shorted signal wire can force the circuit voltage low and set P0117 even if the sensor is good. This is more likely if the code returns immediately after clearing or if the wiring is rubbed through near the thermostat housing.
causes.check: Look for chafed, melted, or pinched wires near the sensor and check for damaged insulation where the harness bends or touches hot parts.

causes.name: Low coolant level or trapped air around the sensor
causes.detail: If the cooling system is low, the sensor may not be fully surrounded by coolant, which can cause odd temperature readings and overheating symptoms. This is more likely if the vehicle is also running hot or the heater blows cold air.
causes.check: Check the coolant reservoir and radiator level when the engine is cold, and look for signs of leaks or recent coolant service.

diy.summary: A home mechanic can often inspect the connector, top off coolant, or replace the coolant temperature sensor with basic hand tools and the correct replacement part. If wiring is damaged or the code keeps returning after sensor replacement, ask the shop to test the harness and computer input circuit.
steps: Let the engine cool completely.
Check coolant level in the reservoir and radiator if equipped.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for corrosion or damage.
Clear the code and see if it returns right away.
If needed, replace the coolant temperature sensor and sealing ring.
Top off coolant and bleed air from the system if the vehicle requires it.
Verify the scan tool reading rises smoothly as the engine warms up.

costs.note: parts about $20-$80, labor about $100-$270
parts about $15-$60, labor about $85-$190
depends on access and how much harness damage is present
usually added if low coolant or air in the system is found

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, engine layout, and local labor rates, and diagnostics may add to the total.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0117?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and get it checked soon. If the engine is overheating, running very rough, or the coolant level is low, do not keep driving.

faqs.question: Will P0117 cause overheating?
faqs.answer: Not usually by itself, but a bad coolant sensor reading can hide a real overheating problem or keep the fans from being controlled correctly on some vehicles. If the temperature gauge is climbing, treat it as a cooling-system issue.

faqs.question: Can a bad thermostat cause P0117?
faqs.answer: A thermostat problem more often sets a different code, such as P0128, rather than P0117. P0117 is more directly about the sensor circuit, connector, wiring, or the sensor itself.

faqs.question: Can I fix P0117 myself?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the problem is a sensor, connector, coolant level, or an obvious wiring issue. If the wiring fault is hidden or intermittent, a shop usually needs to test the circuit with a meter.

faqs.question: Will P0117 fail emissions or inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, because the check engine light is on and the engine may run too rich. Many inspections fail a vehicle with an active emissions-related trouble code.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Circuit High
answer: P0118 means the engine computer is seeing an unrealistically high signal from the coolant temperature sensor circuit, usually because the circuit is open, the sensor is bad, or the connector/wiring has a fault. The most common fix is replacing the coolant temperature sensor or repairing the wiring, typically costing about $120 to $350 at an independent shop.
meaning: The engine coolant temperature sensor tells the computer how hot the engine is so it can control fuel mixture, ignition timing, idle speed, and radiator fan operation. When the signal is too high, the computer often thinks the engine is extremely cold or that the sensor circuit has failed open. That can cause poor running, hard starting, bad fuel economy, and sometimes cooling fan problems. On many vehicles, low coolant level, damaged wiring, or a failed sensor can all trigger this code.
symptoms: Cooling fan running more than normal
Black exhaust smoke or rich running in some cases
safety_note: The car may still run, but fuel mixture and cooling fan control can be wrong, which can hurt fuel economy and drivability. Stop driving if the engine starts overheating, runs extremely rough, or the temperature gauge behaves erratically.

causes.name: Failed engine coolant temperature sensor
causes.detail: A bad sensor is the most common cause when the code comes back right away and the temperature reading on a scan tool stays unrealistic, such as very cold on a hot engine.
causes.check: Compare the scan tool coolant temperature to a cold engine and then after warm-up; if it never changes normally, suspect the sensor.

causes.name: Open or damaged wiring in the sensor circuit
causes.detail: Broken wiring, corrosion, or a loose connector can make the signal jump high or read as an open circuit, especially if the code appears intermittently or after hitting bumps.
causes.check: Inspect the connector and harness near the thermostat housing or coolant outlet for damage, corrosion, or loose pins.

causes.name: Low coolant level or air pocket near the sensor
causes.detail: If the sensor is not fully immersed in coolant, it can read abnormally and set the code, often along with overheating or a fluctuating gauge.
causes.check: Check the coolant level only when the engine is cool and look for signs of air in the system or recent coolant loss.

causes.name: Faulty PCM or reference voltage problem
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring test good but the scan data still looks wrong, the computer or its 5-volt reference circuit may be at fault.
causes.check: A shop can verify sensor resistance and circuit voltage with a multimeter before replacing the PCM.

diy.summary: A sensor replacement can be a reasonable DIY job on some cars if the sensor is easy to reach and the engine is cool. You may need a replacement sensor, coolant top-off, basic hand tools, and a way to clear the code; wiring diagnosis is better left to a shop if the connector or harness looks damaged.
steps: Let the engine cool completely.
Check the coolant level and top it off if needed.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for corrosion or damage.
Replace the coolant temperature sensor if it tests bad or is clearly faulty.
Refill and bleed the cooling system if coolant was lost.
Clear the code and verify the temperature reading on a scan tool.
Road test and recheck for leaks or returning codes.

costs.repair: Wiring repair at coolant temp sensor circuit
costs.note: depends on corrosion, broken wires, or connector replacement

costs.repair: Coolant flush and bleed for low-coolant/air-pocket issue
costs.note: often needed if coolant was lost or contaminated

costs.repair: Thermostat replacement if related cooling issue is found
costs.note: not the code itself, but sometimes done during diagnosis

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle design, labor time, and local shop rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0118?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and watch the temperature gauge. If the engine overheats or runs badly, stop driving.

faqs.question: Will P0118 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may clear temporarily if the connection comes back, but the problem usually returns until the bad sensor, wiring, or coolant issue is fixed.

faqs.question: Is P0118 the same as a thermostat problem?
faqs.answer: No. A thermostat problem can affect engine temperature, but P0118 is specifically an electrical fault in the coolant temperature circuit.

faqs.question: Can low coolant cause P0118?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the sensor is out of the coolant or there is air in the system, the reading can go out of range and set this code.

faqs.question: What should I ask the mechanic to check?
faqs.answer: Ask them to inspect the coolant temperature sensor, connector, wiring, coolant level, and live data from the sensor before replacing parts.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch 'A' Circuit
answer: P0120 means the engine computer is seeing a problem in the throttle or accelerator pedal position sensor circuit, which can confuse throttle control and affect how the engine responds. The most common fix is repairing wiring or replacing the throttle body or pedal position sensor, usually about $150 to $500 at an independent shop.
meaning: The throttle position sensor or accelerator pedal position sensor tells the computer how far you are pressing the pedal or opening the throttle. The computer uses that signal to control fuel delivery, air flow, and sometimes electronic throttle operation. If the signal is missing, erratic, or out of range, the computer sets P0120. On many vehicles, this can trigger reduced power or poor throttle response.
safety_note: The engine may go into reduced-power mode or respond unpredictably, which can make merging or passing unsafe. Stop driving if the engine stalls often, the throttle feels dead, or the vehicle will not accelerate normally.

causes.name: Damaged throttle or pedal sensor wiring
causes.detail: Intermittent hesitation, sudden reduced power, or a check engine light that comes and goes often points to a wiring or connector issue. Wet connectors, rubbed-through wiring, or loose plugs are common clues.
causes.check: Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion, loose pins, broken lock tabs, or chafed wires near the throttle body or pedal assembly.

causes.name: Faulty throttle position sensor or pedal position sensor
causes.detail: A steady poor-throttle response, dead spots in pedal movement, or a code that returns after clearing can point to a bad sensor. This is more likely if wiring looks good and other related codes are not present.
causes.check: Use a scan tool with live data to watch the sensor signal while slowly pressing the pedal; look for sudden jumps, dropouts, or no change.

causes.name: Dirty or failing electronic throttle body
causes.detail: Rough idle, hesitation, or reduced power on drive-by-wire systems can happen when the throttle body motor or internal sensor fails. Carbon buildup alone usually causes driveability complaints, but the code often returns if the throttle unit is failing.
causes.check: Look for heavy carbon around the throttle plate and confirm whether the throttle plate moves smoothly with key-on commands if your scan tool supports it.

causes.name: Computer or reference-voltage problem
causes.detail: If the signal, 5-volt reference, or ground is missing across multiple sensors, the fault may be in the harness or engine computer rather than the sensor itself. This is more likely if several unrelated codes appear together.
causes.check: Check for additional sensor codes and test the 5-volt reference and ground at the sensor connector with a multimeter.

diy.summary: Basic inspection and connector cleaning are reasonable for a careful DIY owner with a scan tool and multimeter. If the problem needs wiring repair, throttle body replacement, or circuit testing, ask the shop to diagnose the sensor signal, 5-volt reference, and ground before replacing parts.
steps: Check for loose, dirty, or damaged connectors at the throttle body or pedal sensor
Inspect the harness for rubbed insulation, bent pins, or corrosion
Clear the code and see if it returns right away
Use live data to watch the throttle or pedal signal while moving it slowly
Clean the throttle body only if contamination is visible and the vehicle uses an electronic throttle body that allows cleaning
If wiring and cleaning do not help, test the sensor circuit with a multimeter or have a shop diagnose it

costs.note: small harness repair, terminals, or connector work

costs.repair: Throttle position sensor or accelerator pedal sensor replacement
costs.note: parts and labor vary by vehicle design
often includes labor and basic relearn procedure

costs.repair: Throttle body cleaning and throttle relearn
costs.note: only if contamination is part of the problem
diagnostic time only; module replacement is less common and costlier

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, engine layout, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0120?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time if the car still accelerates normally, but drive carefully. If the engine loses power, stalls, or the throttle feels unresponsive, stop driving and get it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0120 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away temporarily if the connection is intermittent, but the code usually returns until the fault is fixed. Clearing the code without repairing the cause is often only a short-term reset.

faqs.question: Is P0120 a throttle body problem or a pedal sensor problem?
faqs.answer: It can be either, depending on the vehicle design. The code means the computer sees a problem in the throttle/pedal position sensor circuit, so the exact failed part has to be tested.

faqs.question: Can a dirty throttle body cause P0120?
faqs.answer: Yes, on some electronic throttle systems a dirty throttle body can cause poor throttle movement or signal problems. But a wiring issue or a failing sensor is usually more likely than dirt alone.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to fix P0120?
faqs.answer: Typical independent-shop repairs run about $150 to $500, but wiring damage or a throttle body replacement can cost more. The final price depends on whether the problem is the sensor, wiring, or throttle body assembly.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch 'A' Circuit Range/Performance
answer: P0121 means the engine computer sees the throttle position sensor or accelerator pedal position sensor signal out of its expected range, so it cannot accurately tell how far you are pressing the throttle. The most common fix is repairing a bad throttle body or throttle pedal sensor circuit, which typically costs about $150 to $500, or more if the whole throttle body must be replaced.
meaning: The throttle or pedal position sensor tells the engine computer how much air and power you want. If that signal is erratic, too high, too low, or not changing smoothly, the computer sets P0121. This can happen with a worn sensor, dirty throttle body, wiring problems, or poor connector contact. On many cars, the computer may also reduce power to protect the engine and transmission.
safety_note: The car may run poorly, hesitate, or go into reduced-power mode. If the engine stalls, will not respond to the accelerator, or the throttle warning light comes on, stop driving and have it checked.

causes.name: Faulty throttle position or pedal position sensor
causes.detail: Most likely if the check engine light comes on with hesitation, dead spots in pedal response, or unstable idle. The signal may jump around or fail a smooth sweep test.
causes.check: Scan live data and slowly press the pedal; the voltage or percentage should rise smoothly without dropouts.

causes.name: Dirty or sticking throttle body
causes.detail: Likely if idle is rough, the engine hesitates off idle, or the throttle plate feels sticky from carbon buildup. Airflow problems can make the sensor reading look out of range.
causes.check: Inspect the throttle body for heavy carbon buildup and make sure the throttle plate moves freely.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem
causes.detail: More likely if the code comes and goes, or if there are signs of corrosion, damaged harnesses, or water intrusion near the throttle body or pedal sensor. An intermittent connection can make the signal unstable.
causes.check: Wiggle-test the connector and harness while watching live data, and inspect for bent pins, corrosion, or broken wires.

causes.name: Low system voltage or module issue
causes.detail: Possible if several throttle-related or communication codes are present, or the problem started after a dead battery, jump start, or charging problem. Low voltage can distort sensor readings.
causes.check: Check battery and charging system voltage and look for related codes before replacing parts.

diy.summary: A basic throttle body cleaning and connector inspection can be DIY on many cars, but sensor diagnosis usually needs a scan tool that shows live data. If the sensor is built into the throttle body or pedal assembly, ask the shop to test the signal, connector, and wiring before replacing parts.
steps: Scan for codes and freeze-frame data
Inspect the throttle body and air intake for dirt or damage
Check the throttle/pedal sensor connector for looseness or corrosion
Clean the throttle body if it is visibly dirty and the vehicle design allows it
Clear the code and road test
Watch live data for a smooth throttle signal
If the code returns, test wiring and sensor voltage before replacing parts

costs.note: labor and cleaner; some vehicles need an idle relearn

costs.repair: Throttle position sensor or accelerator pedal sensor replacement
costs.note: parts and labor; varies by vehicle design
many cars use an integrated electronic throttle body
depends on wire damage or corrosion
scan-tool testing and calibration on some vehicles

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, parts quality, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0121?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time if the car still drives normally, but use caution. If it hesitates badly, stalls, or goes into reduced-power mode, get it repaired soon.

faqs.question: Will P0121 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it may stay off for a while if the problem is intermittent, but the fault is usually still there. If the code returns, the sensor, throttle body, or wiring needs diagnosis.

faqs.question: Does P0121 mean I need a new throttle body?
faqs.answer: Not always. The problem can be a dirty throttle body, a bad pedal sensor, wiring damage, or the throttle body assembly itself.

faqs.question: Can a dirty throttle body cause P0121?
faqs.answer: Yes. Carbon buildup can make the throttle plate stick or move unevenly, which can confuse the sensor reading and trigger the code.

faqs.question: Will P0121 cause the car to fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: In most places, yes if the check engine light is on or readiness monitors are not set. The code should be fixed before inspection.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch 'A' Circuit Low
answer: P0122 means the engine computer is seeing a very low signal from the throttle or accelerator pedal position sensor circuit. The most common fix is replacing a bad throttle body or pedal position sensor and repairing the wiring, usually costing about $150 to $600.
meaning: The throttle or accelerator pedal position sensor tells the computer how far you are pressing the gas pedal or opening the throttle. The computer uses that signal to control fuel delivery and throttle response. When the signal is too low, the computer may think the pedal is barely pressed or stuck, so it can limit engine power or set a fault. This can happen from a bad sensor, damaged wiring, corrosion, or a problem inside the throttle body on drive-by-wire cars.
symptoms: Engine may go into limp mode
safety_note: The car may run in reduced-power mode or stall, which can make merging and passing unsafe. Stop driving if the engine loses throttle response, enters limp mode badly, or stalls repeatedly.

causes.name: Failed throttle position sensor or pedal position sensor
causes.detail: A dead spot, delayed response, or constant low reading from the pedal or throttle sensor often sets this code. If the light came on with poor acceleration but no wiring damage, this is the most likely cause.
causes.check: Scan live data and watch the throttle or pedal percentage while slowly pressing the pedal; it should rise smoothly without dropping out.

causes.name: Broken, shorted, or corroded wiring connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, a code that returns after bumps, or a code paired with other sensor faults often point to wiring issues. Damaged harnesses near the throttle body or pedal are common.
causes.check: Inspect the connector and wiring for looseness, corrosion, rubbed-through insulation, or bent pins.

causes.name: Dirty or failing electronic throttle body
causes.detail: On many drive-by-wire vehicles, a throttle body that sticks or has a bad internal sensor can create a low-signal complaint. This is more likely if the idle is unstable or the engine stays in limp mode.
causes.check: Look for heavy carbon buildup in the throttle bore and compare commanded throttle to actual throttle on a scan tool.

causes.name: Low reference voltage or PCM problem
causes.detail: If the signal and wiring test good but the code keeps returning, the computer’s reference voltage or internal circuit may be at fault. This is less common than a sensor or wiring issue.
causes.check: Have a shop test the 5-volt reference and circuit integrity before replacing the PCM.

diy.summary: A careful DIYer can inspect the connector, wiring, and throttle body, and sometimes replace the pedal sensor or throttle body. You will need a scan tool that shows live data, basic hand tools, and the correct replacement part for your exact vehicle.
steps: Read all stored codes and freeze-frame data
Inspect the throttle body and pedal connector for damage or corrosion
Check live data for a smooth throttle or pedal signal
Clean the throttle body only if the manufacturer allows it
Repair damaged wiring or replace the faulty sensor or throttle body
Clear codes and verify the signal returns to normal
Road test to confirm the light stays off

parts about $150-$450, labor about $100-$200
depends on access and amount of harness damage

costs.note: service time varies; may solve sticking issues
diagnosis first; replacement is uncommon

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0122?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently. If the car goes into reduced-power mode, stalls, or barely responds to the pedal, stop driving and have it towed.

faqs.question: Will P0122 cause limp mode?
faqs.answer: Yes, it often can. The computer may limit throttle opening to protect the engine and keep the car from accelerating unexpectedly.

faqs.question: Can a dirty throttle body cause P0122?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, especially on drive-by-wire systems where carbon buildup makes the throttle plate stick. It is not the first thing I would assume, but it is worth checking if the throttle body is dirty.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to fix P0122?
faqs.answer: Typical independent-shop cost is about $150 to $600, depending on whether the fix is wiring, a pedal sensor, or the throttle body. PCM-related repairs can cost more.

faqs.question: Will P0122 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: In most states, yes, because the check engine light is on and the readiness monitors may not be set. The code should be repaired and cleared before inspection.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch 'A' Circuit High
answer: P0123 means the engine computer is seeing an abnormally high voltage signal from the throttle or accelerator pedal position sensor circuit. The most common fix is repairing a damaged connector or replacing the throttle body or pedal position sensor, usually costing about $150 to $500 at an independent shop.
meaning: This code points to a problem in the circuit that tells the engine computer how far the throttle is open or how far the accelerator pedal is pressed. On many cars, that signal comes from a throttle position sensor on the throttle body or a pedal position sensor at the accelerator pedal, depending on design. 'Circuit high' usually means the computer is seeing too much voltage, often from a wiring issue, bad sensor, or a connector problem. Because the computer uses this signal to control fuel delivery and throttle response, the car may go into reduced-power mode.
symptoms: Engine may go into limp mode
safety_note: The car may still drive, but it can lose power or respond unpredictably to the gas pedal. Stop driving if the engine will not rev normally, the car enters limp mode, or the throttle response becomes erratic.

causes.name: Faulty throttle position or pedal position sensor
causes.detail: If the check engine light comes with poor throttle response or limp mode, the sensor itself may be sending a voltage that is too high. This is common when the code returns right away after clearing.
causes.check: Scan live data and watch the sensor voltage or percentage; a reading stuck high or jumping abnormally points to a bad sensor.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or poor connector connection
causes.detail: Intermittent hesitation, sudden warning lights, or the code appearing after hitting a bump often point to wiring damage, corrosion, or a loose plug. A rubbed-through harness can raise the signal voltage or short it to power.
causes.check: Inspect the connector and wiring near the throttle body or pedal for bent pins, corrosion, broken insulation, or loose fit.

causes.name: Throttle body problem or carbon buildup
causes.detail: If idle is too high, throttle response is off, or the throttle plate sticks, the throttle body assembly may be at fault. Some vehicles use an integrated sensor that fails with the throttle body.
causes.check: Check for heavy carbon buildup or a throttle plate that does not move smoothly when commanded by scan tool.

causes.name: PCM or accelerator pedal assembly fault
causes.detail: If the wiring and sensor tests are normal but the code keeps returning, the control module or pedal assembly may be failing. This is less common than sensor or wiring problems.
causes.check: Compare live data from both sensor tracks and follow factory test steps before replacing the module.

diy.summary: A basic inspection of the connector, wiring, and throttle body is doable for many owners with a scan tool and hand tools. If the sensor is built into the throttle body or the pedal assembly, ask the shop to diagnose live data and wiring before replacing parts.
steps: Read all codes and freeze-frame data
Inspect the throttle body or pedal connector
Look for bent pins, corrosion, or broken wires
Check that the connector locks firmly in place
Clear the code and test-drive if the problem was an obvious connection issue
If the code returns, monitor live sensor data with a scan tool
Replace the faulty sensor, throttle body, or pedal assembly only after testing
Perform any required throttle relearn procedure

costs.note: parts and labor, common on vehicles with an integrated TPS

costs.repair: Accelerator pedal position sensor or pedal assembly replacement
costs.note: parts and labor, depending on design
minor harness repair, terminal work, or connector pigtail

costs.repair: Throttle body cleaning and relearn service
costs.note: helpful when sticking or heavy carbon is part of the issue
rare; usually only after wiring and sensor tests

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0123?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short distance, but drive gently because the car may lose throttle response or enter limp mode. If the engine will not respond normally to the gas pedal, stop driving.

faqs.question: Will P0123 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away temporarily if the connection is intermittent, but the problem usually comes back until the cause is fixed. Clearing the code without repair often does not solve it.

faqs.question: Is P0123 more likely the throttle body or the pedal?
faqs.answer: Either one can cause it, depending on the car. A scan tool and wiring checks help determine whether the signal is coming from the throttle body sensor or the accelerator pedal sensor.

faqs.question: Can a dirty throttle body cause P0123?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, especially if the throttle plate sticks or the assembly is worn. But a dirty throttle body is not as common a cause as a bad sensor or wiring issue for this code.

faqs.question: Will P0123 pass inspection?
faqs.answer: Usually not if the check engine light is on, because the vehicle has an active emissions fault. Even if it runs okay, the code should be repaired before inspection.

title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control
answer: P0125 means the engine computer is not seeing the coolant warm up enough to switch into closed-loop fuel control. The most common fix is replacing a thermostat stuck open, which typically costs about $180 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: Your engine starts in open loop, where the computer uses preset fuel settings until the coolant gets warm enough for accurate sensor feedback. Closed loop is the normal running mode, and P0125 sets when the engine stays too cool for too long or the computer cannot confirm warm-up. In many cars, the issue is a thermostat stuck open, so coolant keeps flowing too soon and the engine never reaches the expected temperature. Less often, the problem is a faulty coolant temperature sensor, low coolant, or a cooling system issue that keeps the engine running cold.
safety_note: The car will usually still run, but fuel economy and drivability can suffer, and the engine may stay in warm-up mode longer than normal. Stop driving if the temperature gauge starts climbing toward overheating, coolant is leaking, or the engine runs very poorly.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.detail: This is the most common cause when the temperature gauge stays low, the cabin heat is weak, or the engine takes a long time to warm up.
causes.check: Watch the temperature gauge after a cold start; if it stays below normal on a long drive, the thermostat is suspect.

causes.name: Low coolant level or air in the cooling system
causes.detail: Low coolant can keep the sensor from reading correctly and may cause slow warm-up or inconsistent heater performance.
causes.check: Check the coolant level in the reservoir only when the engine is cold and look for signs of leaks.

causes.name: Bad engine coolant temperature sensor or wiring
causes.detail: If the gauge reading is erratic, very low, or does not match how the engine feels, the sensor or its circuit may be lying to the computer.
causes.check: Compare the scanner coolant temperature reading to a cold engine at startup and after a full warm-up.

causes.name: Cooling fan running too much or stuck on
causes.detail: If the fan runs hard all the time, it can keep the engine from warming up properly, especially in cool weather.
causes.check: With the engine cold, see whether the fan is running immediately and does not cycle off as the engine warms.

diy.summary: A thermostat replacement is often a good DIY job if you can safely drain some coolant and access the thermostat housing. You may need a new thermostat, gasket, fresh coolant, basic hand tools, and a way to bleed air from the system.
steps: Let the engine cool completely.
Check coolant level and look for leaks.
Verify the engine is actually running cold with a scan tool or gauge.
Replace the thermostat if it is stuck open.
Refill coolant with the correct type.
Bleed air from the cooling system.
Clear the code and road test.
Recheck warm-up and coolant level.

parts and labor
if low coolant or air is part of the problem

faqs.question: Can I keep driving with code P0125?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for short-term driving, but get it checked soon. If the temperature gauge starts running hot or the heater suddenly stops working, stop driving and diagnose the cooling system.

faqs.question: Will P0125 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away temporarily if the engine finally reaches normal temperature, but the underlying problem usually comes back. The code will stay stored until the fault is fixed and cleared.

faqs.question: Is P0125 usually a thermostat?
faqs.answer: Yes, a thermostat stuck open is the most common cause on many cars. A coolant temperature sensor, low coolant, or a wiring problem can also trigger it.

faqs.question: Can a bad coolant temp sensor cause P0125?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the sensor reports the engine as colder than it really is, the computer may think closed loop should not start. A scan tool comparison to a cold engine and a fully warmed engine helps confirm this.

faqs.question: Will P0125 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: It can, because the engine computer may not complete closed-loop operation and the check engine light is on. Most inspection stations will reject a vehicle with an active check engine light.

title: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)
answer: P0128 means the engine coolant is staying too cool for too long, usually because the thermostat is stuck open or the coolant temperature sensor is reading incorrectly. The most common fix is replacing the thermostat, which typically costs about $180 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The thermostat helps the engine warm up quickly and then keeps it at the right operating temperature. When it sticks open, coolant circulates through the radiator too soon, so the engine may never reach normal temp. A bad coolant temperature sensor or low coolant can also make the computer think the engine is running colder than it really is. This code often comes on during cold weather or short trips because the engine struggles to warm up.
symptoms: Engine takes a long time to warm up
Cabin heat is weak or slow to come up
Possible coolant odor or coolant loss if there is a leak
safety_note: You can usually keep driving short-term, but a stuck-open thermostat can hurt fuel economy and may cause the engine to run poorly. Stop driving if the temperature gauge starts overheating, the coolant level drops quickly, or you see steam or a sweet smell from the engine bay.

causes.name: Stuck-open thermostat
causes.detail: This is most likely if the temperature gauge stays low, the heater blows cool air, and the code returns after cold starts or highway driving.
causes.check: Start the cold engine and watch the gauge; if it takes too long to reach normal or never gets there, the thermostat is a strong suspect.

causes.name: Low coolant level or coolant leak
causes.detail: Low coolant can make the sensor read colder than normal and delay warm-up, especially if you also notice weak heat or a sweet smell.
causes.check: Check the coolant reservoir level only when the engine is cold and look for wet spots, dried residue, or crusty buildup around hoses, the radiator, and the water pump.

causes.name: Faulty engine coolant temperature sensor or wiring
causes.detail: If the gauge reads oddly, the code appears without real drivability changes, or warm-up seems normal but the light comes back, the sensor or its wiring may be lying to the computer.
causes.check: Compare live scan-tool coolant temperature to a cold engine and then after warm-up; a reading that is clearly wrong or jumps around points to the sensor circuit.

causes.name: Restricted radiator airflow or extended warm-up conditions
causes.detail: This is less common, but very cold weather, long idling, or unusual cooling-system issues can affect warm-up and set the code.
causes.check: See whether the code happens mostly on short trips in cold weather and whether the engine reaches normal temperature on a longer drive.

diy.summary: A thermostat replacement is often a doable DIY job if you have basic tools, the correct thermostat and gasket, fresh coolant, and a way to safely drain and refill the system. If you are not comfortable bleeding air from the cooling system, ask the shop to diagnose the thermostat, coolant level, and temperature-sensor readings.

Check coolant level and inspect for leaks
Remove the thermostat housing
Replace the thermostat and gasket or seal
Refill with the correct coolant mixture
Bleed air from the cooling system
Clear the code and road test
Confirm the engine reaches normal temperature

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0128?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, as long as the temperature gauge stays in the normal range and the engine is not overheating. Get it checked soon because running too cold can hurt fuel economy and heater performance.

faqs.question: Will P0128 cause overheating?
faqs.answer: P0128 itself means the engine is too cool, not too hot. But if the cooling system also has a leak or another problem, overheating can happen, so watch the gauge closely.

faqs.question: Is the thermostat or the coolant temperature sensor more likely?
faqs.answer: The thermostat is more common on most cars. If the temperature gauge and scan-tool reading do not agree, the sensor or wiring becomes more likely.

faqs.question: Can low coolant trigger P0128?
faqs.answer: Yes, low coolant can contribute to this code, especially if there is a leak. Check the coolant level only when the engine is cold and never open the system hot.

faqs.question: Will P0128 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: It can, because the check engine light is on and the engine may not reach proper operating temperature. Many states will fail the car if the monitor is not ready or the light is on.

title: O2 Sensor Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
answer: P0130 means the engine computer has found a problem in the circuit for the upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1, the sensor used to help control fuel mixture. The most common fix is repairing the sensor wiring or replacing the oxygen sensor, which typically costs about $150 to $400 at an independent shop.
meaning: The bank 1 sensor 1 oxygen sensor sits in the exhaust stream before the catalytic converter and helps the engine computer fine-tune air-fuel mixture. When its circuit has a fault, the computer may not get a reliable signal, so it can’t adjust fueling correctly. That can be caused by a bad sensor, damaged wiring, a loose connector, or a blown heater circuit fuse on some vehicles. On many cars, this code can lead to poor fuel economy and rough running, but the exact symptoms vary depending on whether the sensor signal is dead, stuck, or intermittent.
safety_note: The car will often still run, but fuel economy, emissions, and drivability can get worse if the problem is ignored. Stop driving if the engine starts misfiring badly, stalls repeatedly, or the check engine light flashes.

causes.name: Faulty bank 1 sensor 1 oxygen sensor
causes.detail: A worn or internally failed sensor is the most common cause, especially if the light came on with no other obvious symptoms or the code returns after clearing. Fuel economy issues, rough idle, or a lazy sensor signal on a scan tool point this way.
causes.check: Inspect live O2 sensor data; if the voltage is stuck, dead, or slow to change, unplug the sensor and test again to see if the circuit responds normally.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or loose connector
causes.detail: Heat from the exhaust can melt insulation or loosen the connector, causing an open circuit, short, or intermittent signal. This is more likely if the code comes and goes, or if moving the harness changes the reading.
causes.check: Visually inspect the wiring near the exhaust and connector for burns, corrosion, broken wires, or a loose plug.

causes.name: Oxygen sensor heater circuit problem
causes.detail: Some vehicles set this code when the sensor heater is not working and the sensor never warms up fast enough. Cold-start drivability issues or a related heater code make this more likely.
causes.check: Check for related heater codes and inspect the sensor fuse and heater power/ground with a test light or multimeter.

causes.name: Engine running too rich or too lean
causes.detail: Vacuum leaks, fuel delivery problems, or exhaust leaks can make the upstream sensor reading look wrong even when the sensor is okay. This is more likely if you also have lean or rich fuel trim codes, rough idle, or hesitation.
causes.check: Look for additional codes like P0171 or P0174 and check fuel trims, vacuum hoses, and exhaust leaks.

diy.summary: A careful DIYer can inspect the connector, wiring, and fuse, and sometimes replace the sensor with basic hand tools. You’ll need the correct upstream O2 sensor, and on some cars an O2 sensor socket or access from underneath.
steps: Verify the code and look for related fuel trim or heater codes.
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for heat damage, corrosion, or looseness.
Check the sensor fuse if the vehicle uses one for the heater circuit.
Use live data to see whether the sensor signal changes when the engine is warm.
Repair damaged wiring or replace the sensor if the circuit tests bad.
Clear the code and road test the vehicle.
Recheck for pending or returning codes.

costs.note: parts about $50-$180, labor about $100-$220
