faqs.question: Can I drive with P0651?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently. If the engine starts stalling, running very rough, or losing power badly, stop driving and have it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0651 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it may go away if the connection is intermittent, but the underlying fault usually returns. If the wiring or sensor problem is still there, the code will come back.

faqs.question: Can a bad battery cause P0651?
faqs.answer: Low system voltage can sometimes trigger electrical and sensor codes, but P0651 usually points more to an open reference circuit than to a weak battery. The battery and charging system should still be checked if there are multiple low-voltage codes.

faqs.question: Is P0651 expensive to fix?
faqs.answer: It can be cheap if the problem is a loose connector or fuse, but it gets more expensive if a wire has to be traced and repaired. Most independent-shop repairs fall in the $150 to $450 range.

faqs.question: Will P0651 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: Yes, in many states a check engine light with an active code will fail inspection. The code needs to be repaired and cleared before the vehicle can pass.

title: Transmission Control System (Mil Request)
answer: P0700 means the engine computer has detected a problem in the transmission control system and turned on the check engine light to warn you. The most common fix is a scan of the transmission module for its own codes, then repairing the specific sensor, solenoid, wiring, or fluid issue found; typical shop cost is about $150 to $450 for diagnosis, with repairs often ranging from $250 to $1,200+ depending on the cause.
meaning: P0700 is not a detailed fault code by itself. It is a general request from the transmission control system to turn on the malfunction indicator light because the transmission computer has stored one or more deeper codes. In many cars, the transmission may still drive normally at first, but it can also go into limp mode or shift badly if the underlying problem gets worse. The real repair depends on the transmission codes that are stored along with P0700.
safety_note: P0700 itself does not tell you what failed, but the underlying transmission problem can get worse and cause slipping, harsh shifts, or limp mode. If the transmission starts slipping badly, loses gears, or the vehicle will not move normally, stop driving and have it towed.

causes.name: Transmission control module stored another code
causes.detail: P0700 usually appears because the transmission module has set a more specific code for a sensor, solenoid, or internal transmission issue. Harsh shifting, slipping, or limp mode makes this more likely.
causes.check: Scan the transmission module, not just the engine computer, for stored codes and freeze-frame data.

causes.name: Low or dirty transmission fluid
causes.detail: Low fluid or badly worn fluid can cause slipping, delayed shifts, and overheating, which often triggers transmission fault codes. If the fluid is dark, smells burnt, or the problem happens after driving, this is a strong clue.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition using the correct procedure for the vehicle.

causes.name: Faulty transmission solenoid or pressure control issue
causes.detail: A bad shift solenoid or pressure control solenoid can cause hard shifts, slipping, or a stuck gear and will often set a deeper transmission code along with P0700.
causes.check: A scan tool with transmission data can help compare commanded gear and actual shift behavior.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem at the transmission
causes.detail: Intermittent shifting problems, warning lights that come and go, or symptoms after rain or repairs can point to damaged wiring or a loose connector. Corrosion or fluid intrusion at the harness is common.
causes.check: Inspect transmission connectors and harnesses for damage, corrosion, or loose pins.

diy.summary: A basic fluid check and visual inspection can be DIY for many owners, but the real diagnosis usually needs a scan tool that can read transmission codes. If the transmission is slipping or stuck in one gear, ask the mechanic to read codes from the transmission module and check fluid condition first.
steps: Check whether the transmission shifts normally or is in limp mode.
Inspect transmission fluid level and condition using the correct factory procedure.
Look for leaks under the vehicle and around transmission cooler lines.
Inspect transmission connectors and wiring for damage or corrosion.
Read codes from the transmission control module with a capable scan tool.
Repair the specific fault code found, then clear codes and road test.

costs.note: scan tool diagnosis, road test, and fluid inspection
parts and labor, if serviceable on this vehicle

costs.repair: Shift solenoid or pressure control solenoid replacement
costs.note: parts and labor, varies by access and transmission type
small harness repair to moderate electrical diagnosis
only if the module itself has failed or needs programming

cost_note: Prices vary a lot by vehicle, transmission design, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0700?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time if the transmission still shifts normally, but you should get it checked soon. If it starts slipping, shifting very hard, or goes into limp mode, stop driving and have it towed.

faqs.question: Does P0700 mean the transmission is bad?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. It only means the transmission control system asked for the check engine light, so the real problem could be fluid, wiring, a solenoid, or an internal transmission fault.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to check for P0700?
faqs.answer: The first step is to scan the transmission module for its own codes, because P0700 is just a request code. After that, check transmission fluid level and condition and inspect the wiring.

faqs.question: Will P0700 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes the light may go off if the fault is intermittent, but the code usually comes back if the underlying issue remains. The stored transmission code should still be diagnosed even if the warning light turns off.

faqs.question: Can P0700 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: Yes, in many states a lit check engine light will fail an emissions inspection. Even if the light is off, stored transmission codes can still matter if the monitors or readiness status are not complete.

title: Transmission Range Sensor Circuit Malfunction (PRNDL Input)
answer: P0705 means the transmission range sensor is sending an invalid or inconsistent gear-position signal to the computer, so the car may not know whether it is in Park, Reverse, Neutral, or Drive. The most common fix is adjusting or replacing the range sensor or repairing its wiring, usually about $150 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The transmission range sensor, sometimes called the PRNDL switch, tells the vehicle computer what gear the shifter is in. That information is used for starting, reverse lights, shift logic, cruise control, and in some cars the backup camera or dashboard gear display. If the signal is wrong, missing, or out of adjustment, the computer sets P0705. This can happen from a worn sensor, a misadjusted shifter linkage, damaged wiring, or corrosion in the connector.
symptoms: Car starts in the wrong gear or only in Park/Neutral
safety_note: The car may still move, but a bad range signal can cause no-start, wrong-reverse-light, or incorrect shift behavior. Stop driving if the transmission will not engage the correct gear, the car starts unexpectedly in gear, or it slips into neutral while driving.

causes.name: Misadjusted or worn transmission range sensor
causes.detail: This is most likely if the check engine light is on with a wrong gear display, no-start in Park/Neutral, or reverse lights that work only sometimes.
causes.check: Move the shifter slowly through all positions and see whether the dash gear display or reverse lights cut in and out at certain spots.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or loose connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, especially after rain, hitting bumps, or moving the shifter, point to a wiring or connector issue rather than a failed sensor alone.
causes.check: Inspect the connector at the transmission for broken clips, green corrosion, rubbed-through wires, or transmission fluid in the plug.

causes.name: Shifter linkage out of adjustment
causes.detail: If the shifter feel does not line up with the gear indicator, or the car only starts in a certain part of the Park/Neutral range, linkage alignment may be off.
causes.check: Compare the lever position on the transmission to the cabin shifter position and look for excess play or a loose cable.

causes.name: Failed transmission control module input circuit
causes.detail: This is more likely if the wiring and sensor test good but the code returns immediately and multiple transmission-related codes are present.
causes.check: Scan for other transmission or network codes and verify the sensor signal with live data before replacing the module.

diy.summary: A careful DIYer can inspect the connector, wiring, and shifter adjustment, but sensor replacement or precise adjustment may require a service manual and a scan tool. Ask the mechanic to verify the sensor signal and linkage alignment before replacing parts.
steps: Scan for codes and record live gear-position data if available.
Inspect the transmission range sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion.
Check that the shifter cable or linkage moves the transmission lever fully through each position.
Clear the code and recheck whether the gear display and reverse lights work correctly.
If needed, adjust or replace the range sensor according to the vehicle procedure.
Test-drive and confirm the code does not return.

costs.note: labor only or minor labor, sometimes with scan-tool setup
parts about $50-$200, labor about $150-$250
depends on corrosion, broken wires, or pin damage
labor varies by access and vehicle design

costs.repair: Transmission control circuit diagnosis and repair
costs.note: only if the sensor and wiring test good

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, transmission design, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0705?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive carefully. If the car starts in the wrong gear, will not recognize Park or Neutral, or shifts incorrectly, have it towed instead.

faqs.question: Will P0705 keep my car from starting?
faqs.answer: It can. Many vehicles need a correct Park or Neutral signal to allow starting, so a bad range sensor or adjustment problem can cause a no-start.

faqs.question: Can a bad battery cause P0705?
faqs.answer: Low system voltage can sometimes contribute to sensor or module problems, but it is not the most common cause. Check the battery and charging system only if the code appears along with other electrical issues.

faqs.question: Is the transmission range sensor the same as the neutral safety switch?
faqs.answer: On many vehicles, yes or very close. Different manufacturers may name it differently, but it performs the same basic gear-position job.

faqs.question: Will P0705 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: In many states, yes, because the check engine light is on. If the car also has a gear-indicator or reverse-light problem, that can be an additional inspection issue.

title: Transmission Range Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
answer: P0706 means the transmission range sensor is giving the powertrain control module a signal that does not match the gear selector position. The most common fix is adjusting, repairing, or replacing the range sensor or its wiring, which usually costs about $150 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The transmission range sensor tells the computer whether the shifter is in Park, Reverse, Neutral, Drive, or a lower gear. The computer uses that signal to control starting, reverse lights, shift logic, and on some vehicles backup safety features. When the signal is out of range or does not make sense, the computer sets P0706. This can happen if the sensor is misadjusted, contaminated, worn out, or if the wiring or connector has corrosion or damage. Some vehicles will also set this code if the shifter cable is out of adjustment or the transmission has internal selector problems.
symptoms: Hard starting or no-start in Park or Neutral
Transmission may start in the wrong gear or limp mode
Gear display may not match the shifter position
safety_note: The car may still drive, but the transmission can select the wrong range or fail to start in Park/Neutral. Stop driving if it will not start correctly, shifts into the wrong gear, or the reverse lights and gear indicator are acting erratically.

causes.name: Misadjusted transmission range sensor
causes.detail: This is most likely if the code came on after shifter or transmission work, or if the gear indicator is off but the car otherwise drives normally. It often causes intermittent starting issues in Park or Neutral.
causes.check: Move the shifter slowly through all positions and watch whether the dash gear indicator matches every position exactly.

causes.name: Damaged or corroded wiring/connector
causes.detail: Loose connectors, rubbed-through wiring, or corrosion can make the sensor signal jump around, which often leads to intermittent symptoms and a code that returns after clearing. Moisture, transmission fluid, or road salt near the connector are clues.
causes.check: Inspect the harness and connector at the transmission for bent pins, green corrosion, fluid intrusion, or broken insulation.

causes.name: Worn or failed transmission range sensor
causes.detail: If the signal is wrong in more than one gear or changes unpredictably, the sensor itself may be failing internally. This is common when the code returns even after the connector and adjustment are checked.
causes.check: A scan tool with live data can show whether the selected gear reading matches the shifter through all positions.

causes.name: Shift cable or selector linkage out of adjustment
causes.detail: If the shifter does not fully line up with the transmission detents, the sensor may report the wrong range even though the cabin shifter feels normal. This is more likely after cable or shifter repairs.
causes.check: Verify that Park, Reverse, Neutral, and Drive each fully engage without extra free play in the shifter.

diy.summary: A careful DIY inspection can check the connector, wiring, and shift linkage, but sensor adjustment often needs service information and a scan tool. If the sensor is hard to access or the transmission has an internal selector issue, a shop should diagnose it.
steps: Check that the gear indicator matches each shifter position
Inspect the transmission range sensor connector and wiring
Look for corrosion, fluid intrusion, or damaged pins
Verify the shift cable is properly adjusted
Clear the code and road test
If the code returns, test live data for the gear signal
Replace or adjust the sensor as required by the vehicle service procedure

costs.note: labor mostly; some vehicles need calibration
parts about $50-$200, labor about $150-$300
parts and labor vary by vehicle
usually small parts plus diagnostic time
only if the problem is inside the transmission

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, labor rate, and whether the sensor is easy to reach or requires additional calibration.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0706?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time if the transmission shifts normally and the car starts correctly, but use caution. Do not keep driving if it will not start in Park or Neutral, the gear indicator is wrong, or the transmission goes into limp mode.

faqs.question: Will P0706 cause a no-start?
faqs.answer: It can. Many vehicles will not crank in Park or Neutral if the range signal is wrong, even though the battery and starter are fine.

faqs.question: Is the transmission range sensor the same as the neutral safety switch?
faqs.answer: On some vehicles, yes or very similar. On others, the function is built into a range sensor or selector switch assembly on the transmission.

faqs.question: Can I clear P0706 myself?
faqs.answer: Yes, but if the underlying problem is still there, the code will usually come back. Clearing it only helps after the sensor, linkage, or wiring issue has been fixed.

faqs.question: Will P0706 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, especially if the check engine light is on or the transmission issue affects readiness or safety systems. A code that causes a no-start, wrong gear indication, or reverse light failure should be repaired before inspection.

title: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor 'A' Circuit Range/Performance
answer: P0711 means the transmission control module is seeing a transmission fluid temperature sensor signal that is outside the expected range or does not change normally. The most common fix is to inspect the wiring and replace the fluid temperature sensor or internal transmission harness, which typically costs about $150 to $450.
meaning: The transmission fluid temperature sensor helps the computer know how hot the transmission fluid is. That information affects shift timing, torque converter operation, and how the transmission protects itself when the fluid gets too hot. P0711 sets when the sensor reading looks implausible, changes too slowly, or does not match transmission operating conditions. The problem can come from a bad sensor, damaged wiring, low or dirty fluid, or an internal transmission issue that affects the sensor circuit.
symptoms: Transmission may stay in a fail-safe mode
Transmission warning light on in some vehicles
safety_note: You can usually drive short distances, but shift quality may get worse and the transmission may go into a protective mode. Stop driving if it starts slipping badly, refuses to shift normally, or the transmission overheats.

causes.name: Faulty transmission fluid temperature sensor
causes.detail: This is most likely if the light is on and the transmission shifts oddly, but the fluid level and condition look normal. A sensor can read too hot, too cold, or stuck at one value.
causes.check: Scan live data and watch the temperature reading from a cold start; it should rise gradually as the vehicle warms up.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, a reading that jumps around, or a code that returns after bumps or vibration point to wiring trouble. Corrosion, rubbed-through insulation, or a loose connector can break the signal.
causes.check: Inspect the harness and connector at the transmission for oil intrusion, broken wires, bent pins, or loose fit.

causes.name: Low, dirty, or overheated transmission fluid
causes.detail: If the transmission has delayed shifts, slipping, or burnt-smelling fluid, the sensor may be reacting to real overheating or poor fluid flow. Dirty fluid can also confuse temperature readings in some systems.
causes.check: Check fluid level and condition using the correct factory procedure for that vehicle.

causes.name: Internal transmission fault or failed control module input
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring test good but the code keeps returning, the problem may be inside the transmission or in the module reading the circuit. This is more likely when there are other transmission codes at the same time.
causes.check: Have the circuit tested with a scan tool and multimeter; compare sensor resistance to live data and service specifications.

diy.summary: Basic checks like fluid level, connector condition, and visible wiring can be DIY if you can safely access the transmission. Sensor replacement may require removing a pan, valve body parts, or internal harness pieces depending on the vehicle.
steps: Check for other transmission codes.
Inspect transmission fluid level and condition using the proper procedure.
Look over the sensor connector and nearby wiring for damage or corrosion.
Clear the code and road test while watching live transmission temperature data.
If the reading is stuck or unreasonable, test the sensor resistance and wiring.
Replace the sensor or internal harness if the tests fail.
Recheck for leaks and verify normal shift behavior after the repair.

costs.note: parts about $20-$80, labor about $130-$270

costs.repair: Transmission wiring repair or connector service
costs.note: depends on access and corrosion damage
only if fluid is dirty, low, or overheated

costs.repair: Internal transmission harness or related internal repair
costs.note: more labor if the pan or valve body must come off

costs.repair: Transmission control module diagnosis or replacement
costs.note: less common; usually only after testing the circuit

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle design, fluid type, and how hard the sensor is to reach.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0711?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and avoid towing or heavy acceleration. If the transmission starts slipping, shifts very hard, or seems to overheat, stop driving and get it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0711 cause limp mode?
faqs.answer: It can. Many vehicles use a fail-safe strategy when the transmission temperature signal is implausible, which can lead to harsh shifting or limited gear operation.

faqs.question: Can low transmission fluid cause P0711?
faqs.answer: Yes, low, dirty, or overheated fluid can contribute to this code. But a bad sensor or wiring problem is still very common, so the fluid alone should not be assumed to be the only cause.

faqs.question: Is P0711 a sensor or transmission problem?
faqs.answer: It can be either. The most common causes are the sensor itself or the wiring to it, but internal transmission problems can also affect the signal.

faqs.question: Can I clear P0711 without fixing it?
faqs.answer: You can clear it, but it will usually come back if the fault is still there. Clearing the code only resets the warning light; it does not repair the problem.

title: Input/Turbine Speed Sensor 'A' Circuit
answer: P0715 means the transmission control module is not getting a normal signal from the input/turbine speed sensor, which it uses to track transmission shaft speed and shift timing. The most common fix is repairing the sensor circuit or replacing the sensor, usually about $180 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The input/turbine speed sensor tells the transmission computer how fast the transmission input shaft is spinning. That information helps the computer choose shift timing, line pressure, and gear ratio monitoring. If the signal is missing, erratic, or out of range, the transmission may shift poorly or go into a fail-safe mode. On many vehicles the problem is electrical, but a failed sensor is also common.
symptoms: Speedometer or shifting may act strangely
safety_note: If ignored, the vehicle may shift harshly, stay in limp mode, or eventually not shift correctly at all. Stop driving if the transmission slips badly, will not upshift, or the car suddenly loses drive power.

causes.name: Failed input/turbine speed sensor
causes.detail: A dead or weak sensor often causes intermittent shifting problems, limp mode, or a P0715 that returns quickly after clearing. If the code comes back immediately and wiring looks normal, the sensor is a top suspect.
causes.check: Inspect the sensor data with a scan tool or test the sensor resistance/output if the vehicle uses a simple magnetic sensor.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector
causes.detail: P0715 is often caused by broken wires, corrosion, oil intrusion, or a loose connector near the transmission. Symptoms that change when the harness is moved point strongly to a wiring issue.
causes.check: Inspect the harness at the transmission for rub-through, fluid contamination, bent pins, or loose locks; wiggle-test the connector while watching live data.

causes.name: Transmission fluid problems or internal debris
causes.detail: Metal debris can interfere with some magnetic sensors, and very dirty fluid may point to internal transmission wear. If the code appears with harsh shifting or other transmission codes, this becomes more likely.
causes.check: Check fluid level and condition; look for burnt smell, dark fluid, or metal on the pan magnet if accessible.

causes.name: Failed transmission control module or related circuit fault
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring test good but the scan tool still shows an impossible or missing input speed reading, the control side may be at fault. This is less common than a sensor or wiring problem.
causes.check: Compare live data to engine RPM and output speed, and check for power, ground, and reference-voltage issues at the control circuit.

diy.summary: A DIYer can inspect connectors, wiring, and fluid level with basic tools, and some sensors are easy to replace if they are externally mounted. If the sensor is inside the transmission or the wiring diagnosis requires wiring diagrams and a scan tool, it is better handled by a shop.
steps: Check transmission fluid level and condition
Inspect the sensor connector and harness for damage
Clear the code and road test to see if it returns
Watch input speed data on a scan tool if available
Replace the sensor if the signal is missing and wiring tests good
Repair any damaged wiring or corroded terminals
Recheck for codes and confirm normal shifting

costs.note: parts and labor; external sensors are usually cheaper
depends on harness damage and connector condition
helps if fluid is dirty but not if the sensor has failed

costs.repair: Internal transmission sensor or valve body related repair
costs.note: only if the sensor is internal or debris/internal wear is found
diagnosis first; actual repair varies widely

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, transmission design, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0715?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and avoid hard acceleration or towing. If the transmission starts slipping, refuses to shift, or goes into limp mode, stop driving and get it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0715 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may disappear temporarily if the signal comes back, but the underlying problem usually remains. If the code returns, the sensor, wiring, or transmission issue still needs diagnosis.

faqs.question: Is the input speed sensor hard to replace?
faqs.answer: Sometimes no, but it depends on the vehicle. On some cars it is outside the transmission and fairly easy; on others it is internal and the repair is much more involved.

faqs.question: Can bad transmission fluid cause P0715?
faqs.answer: Dirty fluid or metal debris can contribute, especially on magnetic sensors. Low fluid or burnt fluid usually means there is also an underlying transmission problem that should not be ignored.

faqs.question: Will P0715 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: Yes, in many states a check engine light with an active transmission code will fail an OBD inspection. Even if the car drives okay, the code needs to be repaired before the light goes out and monitors reset.

title: Input/Turbine Speed Sensor 'A' Circuit No Signal
answer: P0717 means the transmission control module is not seeing a signal from the input/turbine speed sensor, so it cannot accurately track turbine speed. The most common fix is replacing a failed speed sensor or repairing its wiring, which usually costs about $150 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The input/turbine speed sensor tells the transmission computer how fast the transmission input shaft is spinning. That information helps the computer decide when to shift and how much pressure to use. When the sensor signal drops out completely, the computer sets P0717 and may go into a failsafe mode. This can happen because the sensor failed, the wiring was damaged, or the transmission has an internal mechanical issue that affects the sensor signal.
symptoms: Speedometer may act erratic on some vehicles
safety_note: The vehicle may shift poorly or enter limp mode, which can make merging and passing difficult. Stop driving if the transmission will not shift, slips badly, or the vehicle will not move normally.

causes.name: Failed input/turbine speed sensor
causes.detail: A dead sensor is the most common cause when the check engine light comes on with hard shifting, limp mode, or a complete loss of transmission speed data.
causes.check: Scan live data and see whether turbine speed reads zero or drops out while the engine is running and the car is moving.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector
causes.detail: If the code appears after recent transmission work, water intrusion, or a road debris strike, the signal wire or connector may be open or shorted.
causes.check: Inspect the sensor connector, harness, and nearby wiring for corrosion, fluid intrusion, broken insulation, or loose pins.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid level or internal transmission problem
causes.detail: Some vehicles will set this code if the transmission is badly worn internally or if fluid issues cause erratic sensor readings and shifting problems.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition, and look for burnt fluid, metal debris, or other signs of internal damage.

diy.summary: If the sensor is easy to reach, a careful DIYer can check the connector, wiring, and sometimes replace the sensor with basic hand tools. If the sensor is internal to the transmission or the code points to internal damage, it is a workshop job.
steps: Verify the code and check transmission live data
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Check transmission fluid level and condition
Replace the sensor if it is externally mounted and accessible
Clear the code and test drive to confirm the signal returns
If the code comes back, diagnose the harness and transmission internally

costs.note: parts about $30-$150, labor about $120-$300
depends on harness damage and labor time
only if low or dirty fluid is part of the problem
only if the transmission has internal damage or a failed internal sensor

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, sensor location, and how much diagnostic time is needed.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0717?
faqs.answer: Usually you can drive short distances, but use caution because the transmission may shift harshly, stay in one gear, or go into limp mode. If it starts slipping badly or will not shift, stop driving.

faqs.question: Will P0717 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away if the fault is intermittent, but the problem usually returns until the sensor, wiring, or transmission issue is fixed. Clearing the code without repairing the cause is only temporary.

faqs.question: Is P0717 serious?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is not usually an immediate breakdown code, but it can lead to poor shifting, reduced power, and more transmission wear if ignored.

faqs.question: Can a bad battery cause P0717?
faqs.answer: A low battery or charging issue can sometimes confuse module readings, but it is not the most common cause. Most cases are a failed sensor, wiring problem, or transmission issue.

faqs.question: Will P0717 fail an emissions or inspection test?
faqs.answer: In many states, yes, because the check engine light is on and the code is stored. The vehicle usually needs the problem fixed and the monitors ready before it will pass.

title: Output Speed Sensor Circuit
answer: P0720 means the transmission control system is not getting a correct signal from the transmission output speed sensor. The most common fix is repairing the sensor circuit or replacing the output speed sensor, which typically costs $150 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The output speed sensor tells the transmission computer how fast the transmission output shaft is turning. The computer uses that signal to control shift timing, line pressure, and torque converter operation. If the signal is missing, erratic, or out of range, the transmission may shift poorly or go into a fail-safe mode. On many vehicles, the problem is the sensor itself, damaged wiring, corrosion, or a transmission fluid leak into the connector area.
symptoms: Transmission may go into limp mode
Cruise control may stop working on some vehicles
safety_note: The vehicle may still move normally at first, but bad shift control can get worse and leave you with poor acceleration or limp mode. Stop driving if the transmission starts slipping badly, will not shift, or the vehicle suddenly loses drive.

causes.name: Failed output speed sensor
causes.detail: A dead or weak sensor often causes harsh shifting, limp mode, or a speedometer that drops out intermittently. The code may return right after clearing it.
causes.check: Inspect live data for a missing or erratic vehicle speed signal and test the sensor resistance or signal output if accessible.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, a code that comes and goes, or problems after road spray often point to broken wires, corrosion, or a loose plug. This is especially likely if the sensor tests okay.
causes.check: Wiggle-test the harness, inspect for rubbed-through wiring, bent pins, green corrosion, or transmission fluid in the connector.

causes.name: Low or contaminated transmission fluid
causes.detail: Delayed or harsh shifts along with other transmission complaints can happen when fluid is low, burnt, or heavily contaminated. Some vehicles are more sensitive to fluid condition and connector contamination.
causes.check: Check the fluid level and condition per the factory procedure and look for leaks around the transmission and harness area.

causes.name: Transmission control module or internal transmission fault
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring check out but the signal is still missing, the problem may be inside the transmission or in the control module. This is more likely when there are multiple transmission codes or no sensor signal at all.
causes.check: Scan for related codes, verify power and ground to the circuit, and compare output speed data with input speed data on a scan tool.

diy.summary: A careful owner can inspect wiring, connectors, and transmission fluid, and sometimes replace an external sensor with basic tools. If the sensor is internal to the transmission, diagnosis needs a scan tool and a shop-level electrical check.
steps: Check transmission fluid level and condition if your vehicle allows a safe procedure.
Inspect the output speed sensor connector for looseness, corrosion, or fluid intrusion.
Follow the harness for damaged wiring near the transmission case and under the car.
Clear the code and road test while watching live speed data if you have a scan tool.
Replace the sensor if testing and inspection point to a bad sensor.
Repair or replace damaged wiring or terminals if found.
Recheck for codes and verify normal shifting.
If the code returns with no wiring issue, have the transmission and module circuit tested by a shop.

costs.note: parts about $40-$150, labor about $110-$200
depends on corrosion, splice work, or terminal repair
only if low or contaminated fluid is part of the problem

costs.repair: Internal transmission repair or sensor access labor
costs.note: varies widely by vehicle and whether the sensor is inside the case
diagnostic time plus repair or reprogramming if needed

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle design, part location, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0720?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but drive gently and avoid hard acceleration. If the transmission starts slipping, loses gears, or goes into limp mode, stop driving and get it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0720 cause shifting problems?
faqs.answer: Yes. The transmission computer uses the output speed signal to control shifts, so a bad signal can cause harsh, delayed, or stuck shifting.

faqs.question: Is the output speed sensor easy to replace?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. On some vehicles it is external and easy to reach, but on others it is harder to access or may require transmission fluid removal or partial disassembly.

faqs.question: Can a wiring problem set P0720?
faqs.answer: Yes. Damaged wiring, poor connectors, corrosion, and fluid intrusion are very common causes of this code.

faqs.question: Will P0720 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, because the check engine light is on and the transmission fault may keep the vehicle from passing an emissions or readiness inspection.

title: Output Speed Sensor Circuit No Signal
answer: P0722 means the transmission control module is not getting a speed signal from the output speed sensor, which it needs to monitor driveshaft/transmission output speed. The most common fix is repairing the sensor circuit or replacing the output speed sensor, usually $150 to $450 at an independent shop.
meaning: The output speed sensor tells the transmission computer how fast the transmission output shaft is turning. That signal helps the vehicle decide when to shift, how hard to shift, and whether the transmission is slipping. If the computer sees no signal at all, it sets P0722. The problem can be a failed sensor, bad wiring, a connector issue, or in some cases a transmission or module fault.
symptoms: Speedometer not working or acting erratically
Vehicle may stay in one gear or go into limp mode
safety_note: If the transmission cannot see output speed, shifting can become harsh, delayed, or limited to protect the transmission. Stop driving if the transmission starts slipping badly, gets stuck in one gear, or the vehicle will not move normally.

causes.name: Failed output speed sensor
causes.detail: This is most likely when the check engine light comes on with hard shifting, limp mode, or an erratic or dead speedometer, especially if the problem started suddenly.
causes.check: Inspect the sensor for damage and test its signal with a scan tool or multimeter; if the sensor has power and ground but no output, it is likely bad.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector to the sensor
causes.detail: Intermittent shifting problems, a speed signal that drops out on bumps, or visible corrosion near the transmission connector point to a wiring issue.
causes.check: Look for rubbed-through wires, loose plugs, bent pins, transmission fluid in the connector, or corrosion.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid or internal transmission issue
causes.detail: If P0722 comes with slipping, delayed engagement, or other transmission codes, the issue may be inside the transmission or related to poor hydraulic operation.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition if the vehicle has a serviceable dipstick; burnt fluid or metal debris is a bad sign.

causes.name: Faulty transmission control module or related circuit fault
causes.detail: This is less common and is more likely if the sensor and wiring test good but the code returns immediately or multiple communication/transmission codes are present.
causes.check: Scan for additional codes and verify the sensor signal reaches the module before replacing any control unit.

diy.summary: A DIYer can inspect the connector, wiring, and sometimes replace the sensor with basic tools and a scan tool. You will need the correct sensor location for the vehicle, since some output speed sensors are easy to reach and others are not.
steps: Check transmission fluid level and condition if applicable
Inspect the output speed sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Clear the code and road test to see if the signal returns
If equipped, compare live data for output speed to vehicle speed
Test sensor power, ground, and signal output
Replace the sensor if it has proper power and ground but no signal
Repair damaged wiring or terminals as needed
Recheck for codes and confirm normal shifting

if low or dirty fluid is contributing
only if internal damage is found

costs.repair: Transmission control module diagnosis or replacement
costs.note: diagnosis may be needed before replacement

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, transmission layout, and local labor rates.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code P0722?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but only for a short distance and gently. If the transmission is slipping, stuck in gear, or shifting extremely hard, it is safer to stop driving and have it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0722 cause the speedometer to stop working?
faqs.answer: It can on some vehicles, but not all. Many cars use the output speed sensor data for both shifting and speedometer operation, while others may still show vehicle speed from a different source.

faqs.question: Is the output speed sensor hard to replace?
faqs.answer: It depends on the vehicle. On some cars it is a simple bolt-in sensor on the transmission case, while on others access is tight and diagnosis of the wiring is the harder part.

faqs.question: Can a bad transmission fluid level cause P0722?
faqs.answer: Low or dirty fluid usually does not directly create a no-signal code, but it can contribute to shifting problems and other transmission faults. The fluid should still be checked because related transmission issues can show up at the same time.

faqs.question: Will clearing the code fix it?
faqs.answer: Usually not. If the sensor, wiring, or transmission fault is still there, the code will come back after the car is driven again.

title: Engine Speed Input Circuit
answer: P0725 means the engine speed signal to the transmission control system is missing, erratic, or out of range. The most common fix is repairing a bad engine speed sensor circuit, wiring, or connector, which typically costs about $150 to $450.
meaning: The transmission computer uses engine speed data to decide when to shift and how hard to apply the clutches. If that signal drops out, the computer may not know how fast the engine is turning, so it sets P0725. On many cars, the problem is not the engine itself but a bad crankshaft position sensor circuit, damaged wiring, or a connector issue affecting the speed signal. In some cases the transmission control module or related internal wiring can also be involved.
symptoms: Speedometer or tachometer may act erratically
safety_note: If the transmission cannot read engine speed correctly, shifting can become harsh, delayed, or unpredictable, and the vehicle may stall or go into fail-safe mode. Stop driving if the transmission starts slipping badly, the engine stalls repeatedly, or the car will not move normally.

causes.name: Faulty crankshaft position sensor or engine speed sensor circuit
causes.detail: A weak, failed, or intermittent engine speed signal is the most common reason for P0725. This is especially likely if the engine also runs rough, stalls, or the tachometer drops out.
causes.check: Scan for related crankshaft sensor codes and watch live engine RPM data while idling and revving the engine; if RPM drops to zero unexpectedly, the signal is likely failing.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or loose connector
causes.detail: Heat, vibration, oil contamination, or corrosion can interrupt the speed signal even when the sensor is still good. Intermittent shifting problems, a flickering check engine light, or the code returning after bumps point toward wiring.
causes.check: Inspect the sensor harness and connector for broken wires, pulled pins, corrosion, or oil intrusion, and wiggle-test the harness while watching scan-tool data.

causes.name: Transmission control module or PCM issue
causes.detail: If the sensor and wiring test good but the code stays set, the control module may not be reading the signal correctly. This is more likely when several unrelated transmission or communication codes are present.
causes.check: Check for additional transmission or network codes and verify power, ground, and reference signals to the control module before replacing it.

causes.name: Internal transmission fault or related input circuit problem
causes.detail: On some vehicles, internal harness or transmission-side circuit damage can interrupt the engine speed signal to the transmission. This is more likely if the problem started after transmission work or if there are multiple transmission codes.
causes.check: Inspect for transmission fluid contamination in connectors, signs of recent repair, or continuity problems between the transmission and control module.

diy.summary: A DIY check is reasonable if you can inspect connectors, test wiring, and use an OBD2 scanner with live data. If the fault points to the control module or internal transmission wiring, that is usually a shop diagnosis and repair.
steps: Scan for all stored codes and freeze-frame data.
Check live engine RPM data to see if the signal drops out.
Inspect the crankshaft/engine speed sensor connector and harness.
Look for corrosion, oil intrusion, rubbed-through wires, or loose pins.
Clear the code and road test after any repair.
If the code returns, test sensor power, ground, and signal output.

costs.note: parts and labor
depends on damage and access

costs.repair: Transmission control module diagnosis and replacement
costs.note: includes programming when required
may require pan removal or partial disassembly

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, labor time, and whether programming or more diagnosis is needed.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0725?
faqs.answer: Usually you can drive short distances, but use caution. If the transmission shifts hard, slips, or the engine stalls, stop driving and get it checked.

faqs.question: Is P0725 the same as a bad crankshaft sensor?
faqs.answer: Not exactly, but a bad crankshaft position sensor or its wiring is one of the most common causes. The code means the transmission is not getting a valid engine speed signal, whatever the source.

faqs.question: Will P0725 cause a no-start?
faqs.answer: It can on some vehicles, but not always. More often it causes stalling, hard shifting, or fail-safe transmission operation rather than a complete no-start.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to fix P0725?
faqs.answer: Many repairs fall in the $150 to $450 range, but wiring damage or module problems can cost more. The final price depends on whether the issue is a sensor, wiring, or the control system.

faqs.question: Can a bad battery or low voltage cause P0725?
faqs.answer: Low voltage can sometimes confuse control modules and set transmission-related codes. If the battery or charging system is weak, it should be checked as part of the diagnosis.

title: Incorrect Gear Ratio
answer: P0730 means the transmission computer sees a gear ratio that does not match the gear it commanded. The most common fix is to correct low or dirty transmission fluid, but if the problem is internal or electrical, repairs can run about $150 to $400 for service or $1,800 to $4,500+ for major transmission repair.
meaning: Your transmission uses input and output speed data to confirm that each gear is working as expected. When those speeds do not match the programmed ratio, the computer sets P0730. This can happen from low or burned fluid, a slipping transmission, a valve body or solenoid problem, or bad speed sensor data. The code does not point to one exact failed part by itself.
symptoms: Wrong gear or harsh gear changes
safety_note: If ignored, the transmission can slip more and overheat, which can turn a smaller repair into a much bigger one. Stop driving if the vehicle will not stay in gear, revs flare badly, or you smell burning transmission fluid.

causes.name: Low or burned transmission fluid
causes.detail: Slipping, delayed shifts, or harsh shifts with no other clear symptoms often point to fluid level or condition problems. A dark color or burnt smell makes this more likely.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition if your vehicle has a dipstick or a service procedure for checking it.

causes.name: Internal transmission slip
causes.detail: A flare in engine speed during shifts, slow engagement, or slipping in more than one gear can point to worn clutches or bands. This is common when the code returns quickly after a fluid service.
causes.check: Note whether the engine revs rise without matching vehicle speed during acceleration or shifting.

causes.name: Faulty speed sensor or wiring
causes.detail: If the transmission acts normal sometimes and the code appears with erratic shifting or other speed-related codes, bad sensor data may be the issue. Wiring damage or a loose connector can confuse the computer about gear ratio.
causes.check: Look for damaged harnesses, loose connectors, or related codes for input/output speed sensors.

causes.name: Valve body or shift solenoid problem
causes.detail: Hard shifting, stuck gears, or the wrong gear engaging can point to a control problem inside the transmission. These faults often show up along with inconsistent shift behavior rather than constant slipping in every gear.
causes.check: See whether the symptoms change from one gear to another or improve after the fluid warms up.

diy.summary: A basic fluid level and condition check may be DIY if your vehicle has an accessible check procedure. Anything beyond that usually needs scan data, pressure testing, and transmission-specific diagnosis.
steps: Check the transmission fluid level using the correct procedure for your vehicle.
Inspect fluid color and smell for dark, burnt, or dirty fluid.
Look under the vehicle and around the transmission for leaks.
Scan for related transmission and speed sensor codes.
Clear the code after any simple fix and road test to see if it returns.

costs.note: parts and labor, typical independent shop price

costs.repair: Repair fluid leak and top off transmission fluid
costs.note: depends on leak source and amount of fluid lost
parts and labor if a related sensor is faulty

costs.repair: Shift solenoid or valve body repair
costs.note: varies by transmission design and access
major repair when the transmission is slipping internally

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, transmission type, and shop labor rate.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0730?
faqs.answer: You can usually drive a short distance with caution, but do not keep driving if the transmission is slipping, revs flare during shifts, or it will not stay in gear. Continued driving can overheat the transmission and cause more damage.

faqs.question: Will P0730 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away briefly if the problem is intermittent, but the code usually returns until the root cause is fixed. If the transmission is actually slipping, it will not be a self-healing issue.

faqs.question: Is P0730 a serious code?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can be serious because it often means the transmission is not operating correctly. Some cases are simple fluid issues, but others mean internal wear or failure.

faqs.question: Can low transmission fluid cause P0730?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low, dirty, or burnt fluid is one of the most common reasons for an incorrect gear ratio code because it can make the transmission slip.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to fix P0730?
faqs.answer: A fluid service may cost about $150 to $300, while sensor or control repairs can be a few hundred dollars. If the transmission is slipping internally, major repair can be $1,800 to $4,500 or more.

title: Gear 1 Incorrect Ratio
answer: P0731 means the transmission computer sees first gear slipping or not matching the ratio it expects in 1st gear. The most common fix is low or dirty transmission fluid, but if the fluid is okay the repair can range from a shift solenoid or speed sensor to a transmission rebuild, typically about $150 to $4,500+ depending on the cause.
meaning: P0731 is a transmission code that means the gear ratio in first gear is not what the computer expects. In simple terms, the engine speed and transmission output speed do not line up correctly when the vehicle is trying to operate in 1st gear. That usually happens because the transmission is slipping, the fluid level is wrong, or the control system is getting bad speed information. If it keeps happening, the transmission may start shifting hard, staying in first too long, or going into fail-safe mode.
symptoms: Vehicle may start in a higher gear or limp mode
safety_note: If ignored, the transmission can overheat and wear out faster, turning a minor fluid or sensor problem into major internal damage. Stop driving if the transmission starts slipping badly, will not move normally, makes grinding noises, or the warning light flashes with severe loss of drive.

causes.name: Low or dirty transmission fluid
causes.detail: Shifting problems, slipping in 1st gear, or a burning smell often point to low fluid, old fluid, or fluid contamination. These conditions can prevent normal hydraulic pressure needed for first gear.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition on level ground using the correct procedure for the vehicle. Dark, burnt-smelling, or foamy fluid is a bad sign.

causes.name: Failing shift solenoid or valve body problem
causes.detail: Hard shifting, delayed engagement, or the code returning after a fluid service can point to a stuck solenoid or worn valve body. The computer may be commanding first gear correctly, but hydraulic control is not following through.
causes.check: A scan tool that can read transmission data and command solenoids can help confirm whether the transmission is responding correctly.

causes.name: Faulty input or output speed sensor
causes.detail: If the speed readings are erratic or the transmission shifts oddly without obvious slipping, bad sensor data can make the computer think the ratio is wrong. This is more likely when the code comes and goes or appears with other ratio codes.
causes.check: Inspect wiring and connector condition, then compare live input and output speed data while driving with a scan tool.

causes.name: Internal transmission wear or clutch slippage
causes.detail: Persistent slipping, delayed engagement, and burnt fluid often point to worn clutch packs, bands, or other internal damage. This is more likely if the vehicle still sets the code after fluid, solenoid, and sensor checks.
causes.check: Have a shop perform a pressure test and transmission performance diagnosis; internal wear usually cannot be confirmed with a simple visual check.

diy.summary: Checking fluid level, fluid condition, and obvious wiring damage is reasonable for many owners, but anything deeper usually needs a scan tool and transmission test equipment. Ask the mechanic to verify line pressure, speed sensor data, and solenoid operation before approving major repairs.
steps: Check transmission fluid level using the correct factory procedure
Inspect fluid color and smell for burning or contamination
Look for leaks around cooler lines, pan, and seals
Inspect transmission connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Scan for related transmission codes and live speed data
Clear codes after minor service and road test
If the code returns, have a shop test solenoids, sensors, and line pressure

parts and labor; pricing varies by sensor location and access

costs.note: parts and labor; may include pan removal and relearn procedure
diagnosis-dependent; wiring damage, connectors, or module issues can vary widely

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, fluid type, and how much internal damage the transmission has.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0731?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but only gently and not far. If the transmission is slipping, overheating, or refusing to shift normally, stop driving and get it checked.

faqs.question: Will P0731 go away on its own?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it may disappear briefly if the problem is intermittent, but the underlying issue usually remains. If the code comes back, it needs diagnosis.

faqs.question: Does P0731 mean I need a new transmission?
faqs.answer: Not always. Low fluid, a bad speed sensor, or a solenoid problem can set this code before any major internal damage happens.

faqs.question: Can I clear P0731 myself?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can clear the code with a scan tool, but that does not fix the cause. If the problem is still there, the code will usually return quickly.

faqs.question: Will P0731 fail an emissions test?
faqs.answer: In many states, yes, because the check engine light is on and the readiness monitors may not be complete. Even if it passes tailpipe readings, the light alone can fail inspection in some places.

title: Gear 2 Incorrect Ratio
answer: P0732 means the transmission computer sees the 2nd gear ratio as wrong, which usually points to a slipping transmission, low/dirty fluid, or a valve body/shift solenoid problem. Typical independent-shop repair costs range from about $150 for a fluid service to $1,800 or more for internal transmission repairs.
meaning: The transmission control module compares engine speed, output speed, and gear commands to make sure each gear is working at the expected ratio. When it detects that the transmission is not achieving the ratio it should in 2nd gear, it sets P0732. This can happen if the transmission fluid is low or badly worn, if a solenoid or valve body is not controlling pressure correctly, or if internal clutch parts are slipping. In some vehicles, wiring or speed sensor problems can also confuse the computer and trigger the code.
symptoms: Vehicle stays in one gear or shifts oddly
safety_note: If the transmission is slipping, driving it can quickly make the damage worse and leave you with no usable gears. Stop driving if the vehicle will not accelerate normally, the transmission slips badly, or the fluid smells burned or looks very dark.

causes.name: Low or degraded transmission fluid
causes.detail: A low fluid level, burned fluid, or severely dirty fluid often causes slipping, delayed shifts, and harsh or abnormal gear changes in 2nd gear.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition if your vehicle has a dipstick; look for low level, dark color, or a burnt smell.

causes.name: Faulty shift solenoid or valve body
causes.detail: If the transmission shifts harshly, flares between gears, or seems to miss 2nd gear, the hydraulic control system may not be applying the right pressure.
causes.check: A scan tool can command solenoids and show whether the transmission is responding correctly; a shop can also check line pressure.

causes.name: Internal transmission clutch or band wear
causes.detail: Slipping, delayed engagement, and repeated P0732 codes after a fluid service often point to worn internal parts that can no longer hold 2nd gear properly.
causes.check: If the fluid is full and the problem stays the same, a transmission pressure test and internal inspection are needed.

causes.name: Speed sensor or wiring problem
causes.detail: If the code appears with other gear-ratio or sensor codes, or the speedometer acts strangely, the computer may be getting bad speed data instead of a true gear fault.
causes.check: Inspect wiring near the transmission and look for related codes such as input/output speed sensor faults.

diy.summary: A fluid level check and service may be a DIY job if your vehicle is equipped for it, but most P0732 causes need scan data and pressure testing. If the fluid is low, burned, or full of debris, or if the transmission slips after a service, ask the shop to inspect solenoids, valve body operation, and internal clutch wear.
steps: Check for related transmission codes
Verify the transmission fluid level and condition
Top off or service the fluid only with the correct specification
Clear the code and road-test the vehicle
See whether the code returns during a normal 1-2 shift
If it returns, have the transmission scanned for live data and commanded gear ratios
Inspect wiring and connectors at the transmission
Have a shop perform pressure and internal wear tests if needed

parts + labor; access varies by vehicle
parts + labor; often needs transmission removal of pan
parts + labor; only if the sensor or wiring is the cause

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0732?
faqs.answer: You can sometimes drive a short distance, but only with caution. If the transmission is slipping, shuddering, or not shifting normally, driving can make the damage worse.

faqs.question: Will P0732 fix itself?
faqs.answer: Usually no. If the code was set by low fluid or a temporary electrical issue, it may go away for a short time, but a real gear-ratio problem usually comes back.

faqs.question: Is P0732 always a bad transmission?
faqs.answer: No. Low fluid, a bad solenoid, a valve body issue, or a speed sensor problem can all cause it. Internal wear is common, but it is not the only cause.

faqs.question: Can a fluid change fix P0732?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, especially if the fluid was low, dirty, or badly overheated. If the transmission already slips or the code returns after service, the problem is likely deeper.

faqs.question: Will P0732 pass inspection?
faqs.answer: Usually not if the check engine light is on. Some states will also fail the car if the transmission problem affects readiness monitors or driveability.

title: Gear 3 Incorrect Ratio
answer: P0733 means the transmission computer sees third gear slipping or not matching the expected gear ratio. The most common fixes are low or dirty transmission fluid, a bad shift solenoid, or internal transmission wear, with typical repair costs from about $150 for a fluid service to $3,500+ for major transmission work.
meaning: The transmission control module compares input and output shaft speeds to verify that each gear ratio is where it should be. When it commands third gear but the speeds do not match the expected ratio, it sets P0733. This can happen from low fluid, burned fluid, worn clutch packs, a stuck solenoid, valve body problems, or internal mechanical damage. Because third gear is part of normal driving, the vehicle may shift poorly, slip, or go into limp mode.
symptoms: Engine revs high without matching acceleration
safety_note: If ignored, the transmission can slip more, overheat, and suffer major internal damage. Stop driving if the vehicle will not stay in gear, loses drive, or the transmission fluid smells burnt or looks very dark.

causes.name: Low or dirty transmission fluid
causes.detail: Slipping, delayed shifts, and a burnt smell point to fluid that is low, old, or overheated. This is especially likely if the problem started gradually or after a leak.
causes.check: Check the fluid level and condition on level ground per the owner's manual; look for dark, brown, or burnt-smelling fluid and signs of leaks.

causes.name: Faulty shift solenoid or valve body problem
causes.detail: If the code comes with harsh shifts, stuck-in-gear behavior, or inconsistent shifting, a solenoid or valve body issue is likely. The transmission may act up only when it tries to enter third gear.
causes.check: Scan for additional transmission codes and watch live data for commanded gear versus actual gear; a shop can test solenoid operation and line pressure.

causes.name: Worn clutch packs or internal transmission wear
causes.detail: Repeated slipping in third gear, high engine flare during the shift, and a burnt fluid smell point to worn internal clutches or bands. This is more likely on higher-mileage vehicles or after driving with low fluid.
causes.check: A transmission pressure test and fluid inspection for metal debris or clutch material can help confirm internal wear.

causes.name: Speed sensor or wiring fault
causes.detail: If the speedometer acts erratically or there are other gear-ratio codes, bad input/output speed signals can make the computer think third gear is wrong. This is more likely when the problem is intermittent.
causes.check: Inspect wiring and connectors at the transmission and check for related speed sensor codes or unstable scan-tool speed readings.

diy.summary: A fluid check and top-off may be a reasonable DIY first step if your vehicle has a dipstick and you can verify the correct ATF type. If the fluid is burnt, low again after topping off, or the code returns quickly, the diagnosis needs a shop with scan data and transmission testing tools.
steps: Check transmission fluid level and condition exactly as the owner’s manual specifies.
Look for leaks at the pan, cooler lines, axle seals, and transmission case.
Top off only with the exact fluid spec listed for your vehicle.
Clear the code and road test if the fluid was low and the transmission still shifts normally.
Recheck for the code, slipping, or burnt fluid after the test drive.
If the code returns, stop guessing and have the transmission tested for solenoid, pressure, and internal wear issues.

faqs.question: Can I drive with P0733?
faqs.answer: You may be able to drive short distances, but use caution. If the transmission is slipping, flaring between shifts, or smelling burnt, driving can make the damage worse very quickly.

faqs.question: Will a transmission fluid change fix P0733?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, if the fluid was low, dirty, or the wrong type. If the transmission is already slipping from worn clutches or a mechanical fault, a fluid change will not fix it.

faqs.question: Is P0733 a serious code?
faqs.answer: Yes. It usually means the transmission is not holding third gear correctly, and continued driving can turn a small problem into a rebuild.

faqs.question: Can a bad speed sensor cause P0733?
faqs.answer: Yes, a bad input or output speed sensor can confuse the transmission computer and set a gear ratio code. But on many vehicles, true slipping or internal wear is more common, so testing matters.

faqs.question: Will P0733 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away temporarily if the condition is intermittent, but the underlying problem usually remains. If the light comes back after a short time or after a hard shift, the code needs proper diagnosis.

title: Gear 4 Incorrect Ratio
answer: P0734 means the transmission computer sees fourth gear slipping or not matching the expected ratio. The most common fix is low or dirty transmission fluid, a solenoid problem, or internal transmission wear, with typical independent-shop repairs ranging from about $150 to $3,500+ depending on the cause.
meaning: Your transmission control system watches input and output shaft speeds to confirm each gear is working correctly. When it commands 4th gear but the speed ratio does not match what it expects, it sets P0734. This can happen from low fluid, a failing shift solenoid, valve body problems, worn clutches, or internal mechanical damage. On some cars, a wiring or sensor issue can also confuse the transmission computer and trigger the code.
symptoms: Transmission stuck in one gear or limp mode
safety_note: If ignored, the transmission can overheat and the slipping can get worse, leading to expensive internal damage. Stop driving if the vehicle loses drive, will not upshift, or the transmission fluid smells burned or leaks heavily.

causes.name: Low or dirty transmission fluid
causes.detail: Slipping, delayed shifts, or a burned smell point to fluid level or condition problems. Fourth gear is often one of the first gears to show a ratio error when fluid pressure is weak.
causes.check: Check the fluid level and condition if your vehicle has a dipstick; look for dark fluid, low level, or leaks under the car.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or valve body fault
causes.detail: Hard shifting, stuck gears, or the code returning after clearing it can point to a control problem inside the transmission. A solenoid that does not route pressure correctly can keep 4th gear from applying properly.
causes.check: Have a scan tool check for transmission solenoid codes and compare commanded gear to actual gear during a road test.

causes.name: Worn internal clutch or band damage
causes.detail: If the car slips only in 4th gear or flares during the 3-4 shift, internal wear is likely. This is more common when the transmission has high mileage or has been driven low on fluid.
causes.check: Watch for engine RPM jumping up during the 3-4 shift without a matching increase in road speed.

causes.name: Speed sensor or wiring problem
causes.detail: If the transmission seems to shift normally but the code appears with other shift or sensor codes, bad speed data may be confusing the control module. Intermittent warnings or a code that comes and goes can point this way.
causes.check: Inspect wiring to the transmission and scan for related input/output speed sensor codes.

diy.summary: A careful DIYer can check fluid level, condition, and obvious leaks, but proper diagnosis often needs a scan tool that reads transmission data. If the fluid is low or dirty, fix that first; if the code returns, ask the shop to test solenoids, valve body operation, and internal gear ratio slip.

Look for leaks around the pan, cooler lines, and axle seals
Scan for related transmission codes
Clear codes and test drive to see if P0734 returns

If fluid is low, correct the level and recheck
If the code returns, have the transmission diagnosed professionally

faqs.question: Can I keep driving with P0734?
faqs.answer: You may be able to drive short distances, but it is not smart to ignore it. If the transmission is slipping, getting hot, or going into limp mode, drive only enough to get it to a shop.

faqs.question: Will P0734 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes the light may turn off if the problem was brief, such as a temporary low-fluid condition. If the underlying fault is still there, the code will usually come back.

faqs.question: Is P0734 a transmission problem or a sensor problem?
faqs.answer: It is a transmission ratio code, which means the module sees the gear ratio wrong. The cause can be fluid, a solenoid, wiring, sensors, or internal transmission wear.

faqs.question: Can low transmission fluid cause P0734?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low or burned fluid can reduce hydraulic pressure and make 4th gear slip, which often triggers this code.

faqs.question: Will this pass inspection with the check engine light on?
faqs.answer: Usually not if your state checks for active OBD2 codes or a lit malfunction indicator lamp. Even if the car seems to drive okay, the code needs to be fixed before inspection in many states.

title: Gear 5 Incorrect Ratio
answer: P0735 means the transmission control module has detected that 5th gear is not matching the ratio it expects. The most common fixes are low or dirty transmission fluid, solenoid issues, or internal transmission wear, with typical repair costs ranging from about $150 for a fluid service to $3,500+ for internal repairs.
meaning: The transmission compares engine speed, input shaft speed, and output shaft speed to confirm each gear is doing the right job. When the computer commands 5th gear but the speeds do not line up, it sets P0735. This can happen because the fluid is low or burned, a shift solenoid is sticking, the valve body has a problem, or the transmission clutch packs and bands are worn. On many vehicles, the transmission may go into limp mode to protect itself.
symptoms: Higher engine RPM than normal at highway speed
safety_note: If ignored, the transmission can slip more, overheat, and cause more internal damage. Stop driving if the transmission will not shift, slips badly, makes grinding or burning smells, or the vehicle has no forward drive.

causes.name: Low or dirty transmission fluid
causes.detail: If the problem started with slipping, delayed shifts, or harsh shifting, fluid that is low, old, or burned is a common cause. Dirty fluid can also affect hydraulic pressure and make 5th gear act wrong.
causes.check: Check the transmission fluid level and condition according to the owner’s manual or service procedure. Dark, burnt-smelling, or foamy fluid points to a fluid problem.

causes.name: Faulty shift solenoid or valve body
causes.detail: If the transmission goes into limp mode, shifts erratically, or only has trouble in one gear, a sticking solenoid or worn valve body is likely. These parts control fluid flow needed to apply 5th gear correctly.
causes.check: A scan tool can command the solenoids and watch gear ratio data; a shop can test line pressure and solenoid operation.

causes.name: Internal transmission wear or damage
causes.detail: If the code returns with slipping in 5th gear, delayed engagement, or burnt fluid, worn clutch packs, bands, or seals may be preventing the gear from holding. This is more likely on high-mileage transmissions or after driving with low fluid.
causes.check: A transmission pressure test and inspection of the pan for excess debris or clutch material can help confirm internal wear.

causes.name: Speed sensor or wiring fault
causes.detail: If the code appears with other ratio or sensor codes, or the speedometer acts erratically, bad input/output speed sensor data can make the computer think 5th gear is wrong. This is less common than fluid or hydraulic problems.
causes.check: Inspect transmission wiring and connectors for damage, and compare live speed sensor readings with a scan tool.

diy.summary: A fluid level and condition check is reasonable for many drivers, but most P0735 repairs need scan-tool data and transmission diagnostics. If the fluid is full and clean, ask the mechanic to check solenoids, line pressure, and internal clutch wear before replacing parts.
steps: Check the transmission fluid level and condition if your vehicle has a serviceable dipstick.
Look for leaks under the vehicle and around the transmission case and cooler lines.
Clear the code after topping off or servicing fluid, then road test to see if it returns.
If the code comes back, scan for related transmission codes and live gear-ratio data.
Have the shop test solenoid operation and transmission pressure if the problem continues.

faqs.question: Can I keep driving with code P0735?
faqs.answer: You may be able to drive gently for a short time, but it is not a code to ignore. If the transmission slips, bangs into gear, smells burnt, or stops shifting correctly, stop driving and have it towed.

faqs.question: Will P0735 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes the light may go off if the problem is temporary, such as low fluid or a momentary electrical issue. If the underlying fault is still there, the code usually returns.

faqs.question: Is P0735 a transmission fluid code?
faqs.answer: It often is related to fluid, but not always. Low, dirty, or burnt fluid is a common cause because it affects hydraulic pressure, yet solenoids, the valve body, sensors, and internal wear can also set it.

faqs.question: Can I fix P0735 myself?
faqs.answer: A fluid check and top-off may be doable if your vehicle allows it and you can follow the correct procedure. Most other causes need scan-tool diagnosis and transmission testing, so a shop is often the safer choice.

faqs.question: Will P0735 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: In many states, a check engine light with an active transmission code can cause an emissions inspection failure. Even if it passes temporarily, the fault should still be diagnosed before it gets worse.

title: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit/Open
answer: P0740 means the powertrain control module has detected an open or fault in the torque converter clutch circuit, so the transmission may not be able to lock the converter at cruising speed. The most common fix is checking the transmission fluid, wiring, and the TCC solenoid, with typical independent-shop repair costs of about $150 to $650 depending on the cause.
meaning: The torque converter clutch, or TCC, helps lock the torque converter so the engine and transmission turn closer to the same speed at highway cruising. That lowers heat, improves fuel economy, and reduces slipping inside the transmission. P0740 sets when the control module sees an electrical open or a circuit problem in the TCC system. The issue may be in the solenoid, wiring, connector, fuse, or the transmission control side, and sometimes low or dirty fluid contributes to the problem.
symptoms: Higher-than-normal engine RPM at highway speed
Transmission may feel like it is not fully locking up
Mild shudder or slip during cruise
Transmission may go into fail-safe mode on some vehicles
safety_note: The vehicle will usually still move, but the transmission can run hotter and waste fuel if the converter clutch never locks. Stop driving if the car starts slipping badly, loses forward motion, or the transmission warning light comes on with harsh shifting.

causes.name: Faulty torque converter clutch solenoid
causes.detail: This is the most common cause when the code comes back after being cleared and the car has normal fluid level but no converter lockup at cruise. You may also notice higher RPM on the highway or a light shudder.
causes.check: Listen for a solenoid click if the pan is off, or have the transmission command checked with a scan tool and measure solenoid resistance.

causes.name: Open or damaged wiring/connector to TCC circuit
causes.detail: Intermittent or immediate code return, especially after hitting bumps, working near the transmission, or if the connector is oily or corroded, points to a wiring fault. Symptoms can come and go.
causes.check: Inspect the transmission connector, harness routing, and fuse/relay feed for broken wires, corrosion, loose pins, or rubbed-through insulation.

causes.name: Low, dirty, or wrong transmission fluid
causes.detail: If the fluid is low, burnt, or very dirty, the converter clutch may not apply correctly and the transmission may shudder or slip during cruise. This is more likely if maintenance has been neglected or there is a leak.
causes.check: Check fluid level and condition using the correct procedure for the vehicle; look for dark fluid, burnt odor, or leaks.

causes.name: Failed torque converter or internal transmission problem
causes.detail: If wiring and the solenoid test good but the code remains, and the car has ongoing slip, shudder, or overheating, the problem may be internal to the converter or transmission valve body. This is more likely on higher-mileage units.
causes.check: A shop should perform line-pressure, circuit, and lockup command tests before condemning the transmission or converter.

diy.summary: Basic checks like fluid level, connector condition, and visible wiring can be done at home with simple tools. Solenoid testing, pan removal, or internal transmission diagnosis usually needs a scan tool and transmission-specific procedures.
steps: Check transmission fluid level and condition using the correct manufacturer procedure.
Inspect the transmission connector and harness for corrosion, loose pins, or damaged wires.
Check related transmission and TCC fuses.
Clear the code and road test to see if it returns.
Use a scan tool to command TCC on/off if supported.
Test solenoid resistance and circuit continuity if you have the proper service information.
Repair wiring or replace the solenoid if testing confirms the fault.
If electrical tests pass, have the transmission and torque converter evaluated by a shop.
