faqs.question: Can I drive with U0001?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but only with caution. If the car runs normally and only one warning light is on, you may be able to drive short distances, but network faults can affect starting, transmission, ABS, or stability systems.

faqs.question: What usually causes U0001?
faqs.answer: The most common causes are low voltage, damaged wiring, bad connectors, or a module that is not communicating properly. Water intrusion and corrosion are also common on network codes.

faqs.question: Will U0001 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may go away temporarily if the cause is intermittent, but that does not mean the problem is fixed. If the code returns, the underlying wiring, power, or module issue is still there.

faqs.question: Is U0001 an engine problem or an electrical problem?
faqs.answer: It is mainly an electrical/network problem. The code can affect engine operation, but the root cause is usually in the communication network, power supply, or a control module.

faqs.question: Can a bad battery cause U0001?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low battery voltage or weak charging can trigger communication faults across the CAN network, especially right after a jump start, battery replacement, or extended cranking.

title: Control Module Communication Bus Off
answer: U0073 means one or more control modules have lost communication on the vehicle network, so the scanner cannot talk to part of the car's computers. The most common fix is repairing low battery voltage, bad connections, or damaged wiring, which usually costs about $100 to $400; if a module is faulty, repairs can be $300 to $1,200+.
meaning: Modern cars use network wiring so modules like the engine computer, transmission module, ABS module, and body module can share data. When the network goes 'bus off,' a module stops talking because of a communication fault, usually from low voltage, a wiring problem, or a module that has failed internally. This code is often a symptom of another electrical problem, not the root cause by itself. A car may still drive, but other warning lights and systems may act up at the same time.
safety_note: If ignored, the car may develop more warning lights, no-start issues, or loss of important functions like ABS or transmission communication. Stop driving if the engine stalls, the car will not start, or multiple systems quit working at once.

causes.name: Low battery voltage or charging problem
causes.detail: This is common when the car has many random warnings, a no-start, or the problem appeared after a dead battery or jump start. Weak voltage can knock modules offline and trigger a bus-off code.
causes.check: Check battery voltage and charging output; look for dim lights, slow cranking, or a battery warning light.

causes.name: Loose, corroded, or damaged network wiring
causes.detail: Intermittent lights, codes that come and go, or problems after rain, repairs, or rodent damage point to wiring or connector issues. A bad CAN wire or connector can stop communication across the network.
causes.check: Inspect battery terminals, grounds, module connectors, and exposed wiring for corrosion, looseness, or damage.

causes.name: Failed control module
causes.detail: If the code returns after voltage and wiring checks pass, or if one module cannot be reached with a scan tool, an internal module fault is likely. This may show up with one system dead while others still work.
causes.check: Scan for lost communication with a specific module and compare live data and network codes.

causes.name: Blown fuse or poor ground to a module
causes.detail: A module that suddenly stopped talking after another electrical issue, repair, or short may have lost power or ground. This often comes with one system being completely inoperative.
causes.check: Check related fuses and module grounds with a test light or multimeter.

diy.summary: Basic checks like the battery, fuses, and visible wiring are DIY-friendly, but network diagnosis usually needs a scan tool and wiring diagrams. Ask the mechanic to check module power, grounds, and CAN communication before replacing any module.
steps: Check battery condition and charging voltage
Inspect battery terminals and main grounds
Check related fuses for the affected modules
Look for damaged wiring or corrosion at connectors
Scan for other U-codes and lost-communication modules
Clear codes and retest after repairs

costs.repair: Battery, terminals, or charging system repair
costs.note: parts and labor; depends on whether the battery, alternator, or connections need work
parts and labor; cost rises if harness damage is hard to reach
parts and labor; often a fuse, relay, or ground issue
parts, labor, and programming; some modules cost more

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, location, and how hard the network fault is to find.

faqs.question: Can I drive with U0073?
faqs.answer: Usually you can drive short distances if the car runs normally, but use caution. If the car stalls, will not start, or multiple warning lights come on, stop driving and have it checked.

faqs.question: Does U0073 mean the computer is bad?
faqs.answer: Not always. Low voltage, bad grounds, corroded connectors, or damaged wiring are often more common than a failed module.

faqs.question: Will a battery reset clear U0073?
faqs.answer: Sometimes the code disappears after the battery problem is fixed and the codes are cleared, but it usually comes back if the underlying fault is still there. Clearing codes without repairing the cause will not solve it.

faqs.question: Can a bad battery cause a bus off code?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low voltage during starting, charging problems, or weak battery connections can make modules stop communicating.

faqs.question: Will U0073 fail inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, because it is a network fault and may turn on the check engine light or disable systems the inspector checks. Even if it does not fail immediately, it should be repaired before it causes more problems.

title: Lost Communication With ECM/PCM A
answer: U0100 means the other control modules on the car have lost communication with the engine computer (ECM/PCM). The most common fix is repairing the power, ground, fuse, or wiring problem to the ECM/PCM, which typically costs about $150 to $500, but a failed module can cost more.
meaning: The ECM/PCM is the main computer that manages engine operation and shares data with other modules over the vehicle network. When communication drops out, other modules cannot get the engine data they need, so multiple warning lights or a no-start condition can happen. This code is usually caused by a power supply issue, a bad ground, damaged wiring, corrosion, or a failed control module. It can also appear after a weak battery, jump-start, or electrical repair if network voltage was unstable.
symptoms: Intermittent loss of gauges or scan tool communication
safety_note: If the ECM/PCM keeps dropping offline, the engine may stall, not start, or lose important control functions. Stop driving if the car will not start, stalls repeatedly, or several warning lights come on at once.

causes.name: Blown fuse or lost power to ECM/PCM
causes.detail: A no-start, sudden stall, or several modules going offline at once often points to the engine computer losing battery power or ignition power.
causes.check: Check ECM/PCM and main power fuses, and verify battery voltage with the key on.

causes.name: Bad ground or corroded connector
causes.detail: Intermittent symptoms, bumps making the problem come and go, or water intrusion points to a poor ground or corroded connector at the ECM/PCM or network wiring.
causes.check: Inspect battery terminals, chassis grounds, and ECM/PCM connectors for looseness, corrosion, or moisture.

causes.name: Damaged CAN network wiring
causes.detail: If multiple modules set communication codes or the scan tool cannot talk to the car reliably, the network wiring may be open, shorted, or rubbed through.
causes.check: Look for related U-codes and inspect wiring near the battery, fuse box, harness pass-throughs, and repair areas.

causes.name: Failed ECM/PCM
causes.detail: If power, ground, and wiring all check out but communication is still lost, the engine computer itself may be faulty.
causes.check: Have a shop test module power, ground, and network signal before replacing the ECM/PCM.

diy.summary: Basic checks like fuses, battery voltage, and visible wiring damage are possible at home with a multimeter and trim tools. Actual network testing and module diagnosis usually need scan-tool data and wiring diagrams, so many cases are better handled by a shop.
steps: Check battery condition and terminal tightness.
Inspect ECM/PCM and related fuses.
Look for loose, corroded, or wet connectors.
Check main grounds and battery cables.
Scan for other communication codes in all modules.
Clear codes and see if U0100 returns.
If it returns, test power, ground, and CAN wiring at the ECM/PCM.
Replace the ECM/PCM only after supply and wiring checks pass.

costs.repair: Fuse, relay, or power feed repair
costs.note: parts and labor for a basic electrical repair
cleaning, tightening, or minor wiring repair
depends on harness damage and access
module plus programming and setup

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, location, and how much diagnostic time is needed.

faqs.question: Can I drive with U0100?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but only if the car runs normally and the code is intermittent. If it cranks but will not start, stalls, or loses multiple functions, do not keep driving it.

faqs.question: What usually causes U0100?
faqs.answer: The most common causes are a blown fuse, bad power or ground to the ECM/PCM, damaged wiring, or corrosion at a connector. A failed engine computer is possible, but it is less common than a supply or wiring problem.

faqs.question: Will U0100 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may disappear if the voltage problem was temporary, such as after a weak battery or jump-start. If the fault is still present, the code will come back.

faqs.question: Can a weak battery cause U0100?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low battery voltage, bad battery terminals, or a failing charging system can interrupt communication between modules and trigger this code.

faqs.question: Will this code fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, because the check engine light is usually on and the vehicle may not complete readiness monitors properly. The exact inspection result depends on your state and whether the code returns.

title: Lost Communication With Tcm
answer: U0101 means the engine computer, transmission control module, or another module stopped hearing from the TCM. The most common fix is checking the TCM power, ground, fuse, and wiring, which typically costs $150 to $600 depending on whether it is a wiring repair or module replacement.
meaning: The TCM, or transmission control module, is the computer that helps control shifting and other transmission functions. U0101 sets when another module cannot communicate with it over the vehicle network, usually because power, ground, wiring, or the module itself has a problem. In some cars, a low battery or poor battery connection can trigger communication loss, especially right after a jump start, weak battery, or voltage drop. This code does not always mean the transmission is mechanically bad, but it can cause shift problems if the TCM is offline.
symptoms: Transmission stuck in one gear or limp mode
No-start or crank-no-start on some vehicles
Other transmission or network codes stored
safety_note: If the TCM cannot communicate, the transmission may go into fail-safe mode, shift harshly, or get stuck in one gear. Stop driving if the vehicle will not shift normally, loses power unexpectedly, or starts flashing warning lights along with severe drivability problems.

causes.name: Blown fuse or lost TCM power/ground
causes.detail: A dead TCM usually causes the code with no-shift, limp mode, or multiple module communication problems, especially after a battery issue or electrical repair.
causes.check: Check the TCM and transmission-related fuses, then test for battery voltage and a solid ground at the TCM connector.

causes.name: Damaged wiring or connector at TCM or CAN network
causes.detail: Intermittent shifting, the code returning after bumps or rain, or other U-codes often point to a loose connector, corrosion, or rubbed-through wiring.
causes.check: Inspect the harness and connectors for bent pins, corrosion, moisture, or chafing near the transmission and underhood fuse box.

causes.name: Failed TCM
causes.detail: If power and ground are present but communication is still missing, and the transmission controls stop working consistently, the module itself may be bad.
causes.check: Use a scan tool to see whether the TCM responds; if it does not and the wiring tests good, the module may need replacement or programming.

causes.name: Low system voltage or weak battery
causes.detail: This is more likely if the problem started after a jump start, dead battery, or repeated low-voltage events, and may come with several unrelated electronic warnings.
causes.check: Test battery condition and charging system output, and clear the code after restoring proper voltage.

diy.summary: Basic checks like battery voltage, fuses, and visible wiring damage are DIY-friendly, but module communication testing usually needs a scan tool and wiring diagrams. Ask the mechanic to verify TCM power, ground, network signals, and module communication before replacing the TCM.
steps: Check battery condition and charging system voltage
Inspect TCM and transmission-related fuses
Look for loose, corroded, or water-damaged connectors
Check the harness for damage or rubbed-through wires
Clear codes and see if U0101 returns
Scan for related network or transmission codes
If power and ground are good, test TCM communication at the connector

costs.repair: Fuse replacement or simple connector repair
costs.note: parts and labor for inspection, cleaning, or minor electrical repair

costs.repair: Wiring repair to TCM circuit or CAN network
costs.note: parts and labor depending on harness damage and access
battery, terminals, or charging diagnosis and repair
module cost plus labor and required programming

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, location, and whether the fault is a simple power issue or a module/programming problem.

faqs.question: Can I drive with U0101?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but only for a short distance if the transmission is still shifting normally. If it is stuck in limp mode, shifting harshly, or losing power, drive gently and get it checked soon.

faqs.question: Will U0101 clear itself?
faqs.answer: It may clear temporarily if the voltage problem or loose connection was brief, but the code usually returns if the underlying fault is still there. Clearing the code without fixing the cause usually does not last.

faqs.question: Does U0101 mean the transmission is bad?
faqs.answer: Not usually. This code is about lost communication with the TCM, so the problem is often electrical, a wiring issue, or the module itself rather than internal transmission damage.

faqs.question: Can a weak battery cause U0101?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low voltage, dead batteries, bad terminals, or jump-start problems can interrupt module communication and set this code.

faqs.question: Will it pass inspection with U0101?
faqs.answer: Usually not if the check engine light is on or if the transmission fault affects emissions-related readiness or OBD monitoring. The code should be diagnosed and repaired before inspection.

title: Lost Communication With Anti-Lock Brake System (ABS) Control Module
answer: U0121 means the engine computer and other modules stopped hearing from the ABS control module. The most common fix is to diagnose the ABS module power, ground, wiring, or a failed module, which usually costs about $150 to $1,500 depending on whether it is a wiring repair or module replacement/programming.
meaning: The ABS control module manages wheel-speed data and helps prevent wheel lockup during hard braking. When the vehicle loses communication with that module, the warning lights may come on and other systems like traction control can also be affected. This code does not always mean the ABS module itself is bad; it can also happen from low voltage, a blown fuse, damaged wiring, or a network communication issue. On many cars, the problem shows up after a dead battery, jump start, water intrusion, or other electrical trouble.
symptoms: No ABS operation during hard braking
Other network or module codes stored
safety_note: Normal braking usually still works, but anti-lock brakes and traction control may not. If the brake warning light is on, the pedal feels soft, or braking changes suddenly, stop driving and have it towed.

causes.name: Blown fuse or lost power to ABS module
causes.detail: If the ABS light came on after a battery issue, jump start, or electrical repair, the module may have lost its power supply. This is common when the scan tool also cannot talk to the ABS module at all.
causes.check: Check ABS-related fuses and compare battery voltage with the engine off and running.

causes.name: Damaged ABS wiring or connector
causes.detail: Intermittent warning lights, codes that come and go, or problems after hitting a pothole or doing brake work point to a wiring or connector fault. Corrosion, broken wires, or loose plugs near the module or wheel areas can interrupt communication.
causes.check: Inspect the ABS module connector, main harness, and nearby grounds for corrosion, looseness, or damage.

causes.name: Failed ABS control module
causes.detail: If power, ground, and wiring check out but the scan tool still cannot communicate, the module itself may have failed. This is more likely when the code stays set and no other obvious electrical problem is found.
causes.check: Use a professional scan tool to test for ABS communication and verify module power and ground before replacement.

causes.name: Low system voltage or weak battery
causes.detail: A weak battery or charging problem can trigger network communication codes across several modules, especially after starting issues. If other warning lights appeared at the same time, voltage is a strong clue.
causes.check: Load-test the battery and check charging voltage at the battery terminals.

diy.summary: Basic checks like fuses, battery voltage, and visible wiring inspection are reasonable at home. Module testing, ABS wiring diagnosis, and programming usually require a scan tool and sometimes a shop.
steps: Check for other warning lights or related codes.
Inspect ABS fuses and battery terminals.
Verify battery and charging system voltage.
Look for damaged wiring or loose connectors at the ABS module.
Clear the code and see if it returns after a short drive.
If the code returns, have the ABS module communication circuit tested.

costs.repair: Replace blown fuse or repair simple power feed
costs.note: parts low, usually brief labor
diagnosis plus wiring repair

costs.repair: Replace ABS wheel speed sensor wiring affected by harness damage
costs.note: if the communication issue is from a damaged related harness
parts and labor, often includes programming
if low voltage caused the communication fault

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, rust level, and whether the module needs coding or programming after replacement.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code U0121?
faqs.answer: Usually you can drive short distances, but caution is advised because ABS and traction control may not work. If the brake warning light is on or braking feels abnormal, do not keep driving.

faqs.question: Will U0121 clear itself?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it can disappear after a low-voltage event or temporary connection problem is fixed. If the underlying fault is still there, the code will come back.

faqs.question: Is U0121 always a bad ABS module?
faqs.answer: No. A blown fuse, weak battery, corrosion, damaged wiring, or a bad ground can cause the same code. The module should be tested before replacing it.

faqs.question: Can I fix U0121 myself?
faqs.answer: You can check battery condition, fuses, and visible wiring yourself. But module testing and ABS network diagnosis often need a professional scan tool.

faqs.question: Will U0121 make my car fail inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, especially if the ABS light or brake warning light is on. Inspection rules vary by state, but an active ABS communication fault is often a problem.

title: Lost Communication With Body Control Module
answer: U0140 means the powertrain or another module lost communication with the Body Control Module (BCM), which controls many body and convenience functions like locks, lights, and security. The most common fix is to repair a power, ground, fuse, or wiring issue to the BCM, which typically costs about $150 to $600, while BCM replacement can run about $400 to $1,200+.
meaning: The BCM is a computer that helps run non-engine features such as interior lights, power locks, security, keyless entry, warning chimes, and sometimes parts of the wiper or lighting systems. Code U0140 sets when another module can no longer hear the BCM on the vehicle network. That can happen if the BCM lost power, lost ground, has corroded connectors, or the communication wire is damaged. In some cases, the BCM itself has failed, but wiring and power supply problems are usually checked first.
symptoms: Power locks or interior lights not working right
Other network or communication codes stored
safety_note: The car may still run, but you can lose lights, locks, security functions, or other body-control features. Stop driving if the vehicle has major electrical failures, stalling, no-start, smoke, or the battery keeps going dead.

causes.name: Blown BCM fuse or lost power feed
causes.detail: If several BCM-controlled features quit at once, or the code appeared after a battery jump, dead battery, or fuse event, a missing power supply is likely.
causes.check: Check the BCM-related fuses and verify battery voltage is healthy before replacing parts.

causes.name: Bad BCM ground or corroded connector
causes.detail: Intermittent operation, random feature failures, or a code that comes and goes often points to a loose ground, water intrusion, or corrosion at the BCM connector.
causes.check: Inspect the BCM connectors for moisture, green corrosion, bent pins, or a loose ground strap.

causes.name: Damaged communication wiring on the network
causes.detail: If multiple modules have communication codes or the problem started after collision repair, rodent damage, or work under the dash, the network wiring may be open or shorted.
causes.check: Look for rubbed-through or pinched wiring near the BCM, under-dash harness, and splice points.

causes.name: Failed BCM
causes.detail: If power, ground, and wiring all test good but the BCM still will not communicate, the module itself may be bad.
causes.check: Use a scan tool to see whether the BCM responds and compare live data with a known-good power and ground supply.

diy.summary: You may be able to check fuses, battery voltage, and visible connectors with basic tools, but network diagnosis and module testing often need wiring diagrams and a scan tool. Ask the mechanic to verify BCM power, ground, and network communication before replacing the module.
steps: Check battery condition and charging voltage.
Inspect BCM-related fuses and replace any blown fuse with the correct rating.
Unplug and inspect accessible BCM connectors for corrosion or water damage.
Check the BCM ground points for looseness or rust.
Scan for other communication codes in all modules.
Clear the code and see if it returns after a short drive.
If the BCM still will not communicate, have the wiring and module tested professionally.

costs.repair: Fuse, power, or ground repair to BCM circuit
costs.note: diagnosis, minor wiring repair, and labor

costs.repair: Connector cleaning or repair at BCM
costs.note: cleaning, pin repair, or connector service
used or new module plus programming; some vehicles cost more

faqs.question: Can I drive with U0140?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, but use caution. The car may lose convenience or lighting functions, and you should fix it soon if the code keeps coming back or more electrical problems appear.

faqs.question: Will U0140 cause a no-start?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but not usually by itself. If the BCM helps with security or key authorization on your vehicle, a BCM communication failure can contribute to a no-start condition.

faqs.question: What is the most common fix for U0140?
faqs.answer: Checking BCM fuses, grounds, connectors, and wiring is the first step. Many times the problem is a power or communication issue, not a bad module.

faqs.question: Can a dead battery cause U0140?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low voltage, jump-start problems, or battery replacement can trigger communication codes, especially if the BCM briefly lost power.

faqs.question: Will a BCM replacement fix U0140?
faqs.answer: Only if the BCM itself has failed. Most shops should verify power, ground, and network wiring first because the module often is not the root cause.

title: Lost Communication With Instrument Panel Cluster (IPC) Control Module
answer: U0155 means the engine computer and other modules have lost communication with the instrument panel cluster, which can affect the gauges, warning lights, and other dash functions. The most common fix is repairing power, ground, or wiring issues to the cluster, which usually costs about $150 to $600 at an independent shop.
meaning: The instrument panel cluster is the module behind your gauges and many warning lights in the dash. It talks to the rest of the vehicle over a network, and U0155 sets when that communication stops. The problem can be caused by a dead cluster, a blown fuse, low battery voltage, corrosion, damaged wiring, or a network issue elsewhere in the car. In some vehicles, the dash may work only part of the time or stop working completely.
symptoms: Battery light or other module warnings
safety_note: If the cluster is offline, you may lose speed, fuel, temperature, or warning-light information, which can make the car unsafe to monitor. Stop driving if the dash goes completely dead, the car stalls, or you see multiple warning lights with other electrical problems.

causes.name: Blown fuse or lost cluster power
causes.detail: If the dash went dead suddenly or the cluster is completely blank, a fuse or power feed problem is very likely. This is especially common if other accessories or interior electrical items also acted up.
causes.check: Check the owner’s manual fuse panel labels and inspect the cluster and ignition-related fuses for a break or signs of heat.

causes.name: Poor ground or damaged wiring at the cluster
causes.detail: Intermittent gauges, a flickering display, or a cluster that works when the dash is tapped points to wiring or ground trouble. Moisture intrusion or prior dash work can also make this more likely.
causes.check: Gently wiggle the dash harness with the key on and see whether the cluster cuts in and out.

causes.name: Failed instrument panel cluster module
causes.detail: A cluster that has no response even with good power and ground may have an internal failure. This is more likely if scan tools cannot communicate with the IPC but other modules are online.
causes.check: Use a scan tool to see whether the IPC responds and whether other modules report the same loss of communication code.

causes.name: Low battery voltage or network problem elsewhere
causes.detail: If the code appeared after a weak battery, jump-start, charging issue, or multiple low-voltage codes, the network may have dropped communication temporarily. This often comes with other U-codes or module communication complaints.
causes.check: Test battery voltage and charging system output, then check for additional communication codes in other modules.

diy.summary: Basic checks like fuses, battery voltage, and visible wiring inspection are DIY-friendly, but diagnosing module communication usually needs a scan tool and wiring diagrams. If power and ground are present at the cluster and it still will not communicate, ask the mechanic to test the IPC module and the network wiring.
steps: Check whether the dash is completely dead or only some gauges are failing.
Inspect the related fuses for the cluster, ignition, and body control system.
Test battery voltage and charging system voltage.
Look for loose connectors, water intrusion, or damaged wiring behind the dash.
Scan all modules for additional communication or low-voltage codes.
If power, ground, and wiring are good, replace or repair the instrument cluster as needed.

costs.note: inspection plus minor electrical repair
diagnosis, connector repair, or harness repair

costs.repair: Instrument panel cluster module repair or replacement
costs.note: parts and labor; programming may add cost
if low voltage caused the communication loss
diagnosis only, not including repairs

cost_note: Prices vary by vehicle, access time, and whether programming or module coding is needed.

faqs.question: Can I drive with code U0155?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for a short time, but use caution if the speedometer, warning lights, or other gauges are not working. If the dash is dead or the car has other electrical problems, get it checked before driving far.

faqs.question: What usually causes U0155?
faqs.answer: The most common causes are loss of power or ground to the cluster, wiring damage, low battery voltage, or a failed instrument panel cluster. Less often, the issue is a network problem elsewhere in the vehicle.

faqs.question: Can I clear U0155 myself?
faqs.answer: You can clear the code, but it will come back if the communication problem is still there. Clearing the code without fixing the electrical issue usually does not solve anything.

faqs.question: Will U0155 fail an inspection?
faqs.answer: It can, especially if the warning lights or gauges are inoperative or the car has an illuminated malfunction indicator light. Inspection results depend on your state and the exact symptoms.

faqs.question: Do I need a new instrument cluster?
faqs.answer: Not always. Many cases are caused by fuses, connectors, ground faults, or wiring problems, so those should be checked first before replacing the cluster.
